Well, whaddaya know? Turns out all you need to make a great videogame is around a decade of time, the GDP of a BRICS nation, and a marketing machine pervasive to the point of totalitarianism. The reviews for Grand Theft Auto 6—Rockstar's sequel to that game that would splash "GOURANGA!" on the screen when you ran over enough people—are in. People like it a lot.

No, really, they're out of their gourd for this one, folks. GTA 6 might just be the most absurdly hyped game in history, and yet the mad lads at Rockstar really seem to have pulled it off. Of course, the game's true test—its review on PC Gamer dot com and its accompanying magazine—hasn't happened yet. We'll have to wait for the all-but-certain PC port for that. For now, you can read our impressions of the console version here.

But our console brethren have been putting pen to paper to get their thoughts down, and the reviews for GTA 6 are flowing thick and fast. Here's a sample platter of them, to give you an idea of just how nuts people are going for this thing.

GameSpot's Tamoor Hussain paints a picture of Leonida that overflows with detail, calling it "a game of staggering scope and scale obsessed with small details that could be lost in its vastness, a giant haystack full of needles that you’ll constantly find, creating delight in their improbable discovery". I get the impression that a year from now, five years, ten years, there will still be people rushing to subreddits and forums (if we still have those) to ask if others have seen this or that little detail Rockstar tucked into some obscure corner of its humungous world.

A second perfect score from the gang at IGN, whose Luke Reilly had a great time doing things like:

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Most of which you could feasibly cram into a game whose goal was to simulate my dad, but in GTA 6 it all forms part of a world that constantly surprises you with things to do. "I see no real limit to the amount of time I could spend here, endlessly exploring and interacting with Vice City and the massive area surrounding it", writes Reilly, adding that—despite having beaten the game with 120 hours of playtime under his belt—"While the well-paced story effectively nudged me around the map, there are still vast sections of it that I’m yet to even visit".

Our brothers in arms at GR note that GTA 6 is an improvement on every entry in the series before it: "there's no aspect of the series' gameplay that hasn't been improved over past instalments", writes Josh West, who calls the game (affectionately) "the ultimate time vampire" where "every one of your actions ultimately impacts the lives of Jason and Lucia". Honestly, sounds like a nerve-wracking amount of responsibility for me.

The New York Times – Too stately to give a review score but it's an "NYT Critic’s Pick"

You know a videogame has broken containment when the grey lady is getting in on the review beat. The NYT's Yussef Cole zeroed in on GTA 6's heart in his review: the relationship between protagonists Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos—"This is a game about love and relationships, their joy and heartache, and the work required to make them successful", he writes, noting that players can choose to hold hands with their paramour at the touch of a button. We've come a little ways from beating people to death with dildos, folks (though you may well still be able to do that; I'd be surprised if you couldn't).

Giant Bomb (shoutout to Charlie Tunoku) joins in with the hosannahs for GTA 6, describing it as one of those games that feels like a step up for the medium as a whole. "Grand Theft Auto VI is Rockstar’s best game", writes Dan Ryckert. "In the thirteen years between entries of one of the biggest franchises in entertainment, fans’ expectations grew to a level that felt unrealistic. Somehow, Rockstar has managed to overdeliver on the most hyped video game of all time".

The Guardian's Keza MacDonald writes that Rockstar's Leonida is so realistic as to defy belief, but that in its humid, gator-ridden byways you will find scope for both "foulmouthed, OTT chaos—as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre". It is a game, it seems, that is almost too big and varied to squeeze into something like a regular review. "it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start". But you bet those experiences are many, varied, and shockingly fleshed-out.

Bloomberg – Unscored, but you get the picture

Bloomberg's Jason Schreier, who you may recognise from videogame scoops, is in love with GTA 6 too. He opens with a description of one of the random events that can happen to players in the game, in which he witnessed a crash and found himself enlisted into an NPC's scam to sue a parody of Amazon for millions. "Incidents like this, elaborate depictions of a heightened reality, happen constantly in Grand Theft Auto 6", he writes. "The joy of Grand Theft Auto VI, much like The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and Elden Ring before it, comes from discovering its world’s delights and seeing how it reacts to your actions".

It perhaps tells us something that the only non-perfect score on this list is… a 4.5/5 overflowing with praise. Slant's Justin Clark calls GTA 6 "something above and beyond anything the AAA gaming space has ever produced", and has oodles of praise for its rich and hyper-detailed open world. He also thinks that, you know, what's an open world compared to the "first truly meaningful interactive relationship between two semi-realistic grown-ass adults in the entire medium", which Rockstar has also managed to pull off here. "Home, for Jason and Lucia, is each other. Whether there’s $2 million or $2 in their bank accounts, and whether they got it from an honest job or by decimating a metropolitan police force with a grenade launcher, letting these two make a home in each other is the only investment that truly matters—and the best one Rockstar could have ever made, creatively."

One of Josh's first memories is of playing Quake 2 on the family computer when he was much too young to be doing that, and he's been irreparably game-brained ever since. His writing has been featured in Vice, Fanbyte, and the Financial Times. He'll play pretty much anything, and has written far too much on everything from visual novels to Assassin's Creed. His most profound loves are for CRPGs, immersive sims, and any game whose ambition outstrips its budget. He thinks you're all far too mean about Deus Ex: Invisible War.

#3832. While soulslikes went bigger than big, Death's Door swung open the appeal of a tighter adventure

Declaring a Best Way of Doing Things is a fool’s game, though in recent years my favourite entries in the Tricky Hitting genre – inclusive of soulslikes and their hybridised disciples – have been the big, bulging ones. Elden Rings and Silksongs, with vast kingdoms and deep, rattling toolkits for surviving them. The reason it’s a fool’s game is because you can also have something like Death’s Door, a taut, compact, lighthearted little actioner that fills eight hours instead of 80 and yet never feels underwhelming or compromised for it.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

Even in the latter stages, with a full kit of precisely four ranged spells, Death’s Door is a simple proposition. You are a crow. You hit things. Occasionally you shoot things. You collect the souls of a frog, a yeti, and a grandmother. Everything in-between directly relates to finding the errant monster/pensioner, or at a stretch, upgrading one of those four abilities.

Still, it’s clever with its limitations. Environments are small in number but vary wildly in tone and texture, and they tightly weave their paths into criss-crossing bundles that maximise travel – evoking the sense of a great, ranging adventure within relatively tiny spaces. The lack of a wiki’s worth of combat options also never becomes a problem, partly because it spreads out its spell unlocks, and partly because the smooth, flowing back-and-forths of its central swordplay are pleasurable enough to carry it anyway. Good bosses, too! They’re all characterful, memorable weirdoes who fight unlike anyone in their minion armies, and usually come with a hidden weakness to deduce and exploit.

Which is welcome, as these big lads and lasses do tend to launch difficulty spikes right up your feathered backside, and do so in a game that isn’t otherwise as fussed about trial-and-error pain endurance as some of its inspirations. They don’t, however, bring the mood down. At times, this tale of a pitch-black soul reaper working as an agent of Death (complete with an office of Death and embittered co-workers of Death) can get downright cosy, leading through you through warmly-lit jungles and breezy waterside ruins.

Recently replaying, I’d also forgotten how witty it can be. Little gaglets are sprinkled throughout, both visual and verbal, but the best jokes are saved for – funnily enough – the bosses, who’ll raise your pre-fight spirit with some amusingly terrible trash talk before becoming the punchline themselves. I audibly wheezed the first time a death animation immediately cut to the foe’s impromptu funeral, their beaked killer among the precious few guests. And even when the joke is recycled later, I couldn’t help tittering at the sight of my enemy – who seconds earlier, had been attempting to fatally sit on me – lying nobly in state.

I previously considered ending my Valor Mortis review by calling it a gateway into the more demanding side of action-RPGs; a shorter, simpler alternative to FromSoft’s overwhelming titans that might nonetheless serve to introduce curious newcomers to their shared quirks and qualities. The game equivalent of splashing your chest with water before jumping into a pool. In hindsight, Death’s Door was always a better fit for that description, though there’s enough else here you don’t need to be prepping for something tougher to appreciate its lean, keen adventuring.

#3831. Nvidia board considering ousting CEO Jensen Huang, report claims, as news of a second affair comes to light

Nvidia's board of directors has reportedly met to decide whether to remove the company's embattled CEO Jensen Huang, as news of a second extramarital affair has come to light.

Per the Wall Street Journal, the board met on Wednesday to decide whether to remove Huang following reports he allegedly participated in another affair with an executive who worked for him.This followed the revelation of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which prompted a company-wide apology from Huang and an independent investigation into whether he'd been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort".

The board's decision has yet to be made, but there are three expected outcomes. Either Huang stays with the company and continues as Nvidia leader, despite the controversy or he is replaced as CEO, or he quits. Nvidia's share price dropped following reports of this meeting taking place.

If Huang is fired - and perhaps even if he isn't - it's likely to severely disrupt Nvidia's operations. Huang co-founded Nvidia and led it to become one of the world's most valuable companies - it interchangeably wears that crown, alternating with Apple. Replacing Huang might change the company's focus.

Regardless, Nvidia is under major scrutiny right now because of Huang's actions. There are particular concerns around the company's chips being imported to China despite trade bans. Gamers Nexus produced a documentary on the Nvidia AI GPU Black Market, detailing much of this.

#3830. Phasmophobia ‘Resonance’ update launches November 24

Kinetic Games will release the “Resonance” update for Phasmophobia on November 14, which introduces new investigation equipment, technical upgrades, and several gameplay improvements.

“We want to ensure every item in our Ghost Hunters’ kits can add as much value as possible in investigations, and the ‘Resonance’ update has been an exciting opportunity not only to freshen up Sound Sensors and Voice Recognition, but to add a completely new piece of equipment with the Dowsing Rods,” said Kinetic Games CEO and game director Daniel Knight in a press release. “We’re looking forward to hearing how the community get on with them. ‘Resonance’ also brings Phasmophobia‘s move to Unity 6—while this transition is a technical upgrade first and foremost, it has allowed us to implement major lighting improvements to make the game even more immersive. It’s been a huge undertaking for our whole team, and we hope our players enjoy everything ‘Resonance’ has to offer.”

Here is a brief overview of the update, via Kinetic Games:

The “Resonance” update also marks Phasmophobia‘s transition to the Unity 6 engine, bringing technical improvements in the form of more realistic lighting to enhance immersion, and improved stability. Additional settings are being introduced to the game too, with expanded graphics and quality options, VR Eye Adaptation, and a suite of colour-blindness accessibility settings.

Addressing recent community feedback, “Resonance” will also be bringing numerous fixes for several prominent bugs. The update will also introduce a new player conduct warning system that will warn players before receiving an account ban, except in cases of severe violations. Full details are available in the blog notes here.

Phasmophobia is currently in Early Access for PlayStation 5 with PlayStation VR2 support, Xbox Series, and PC via Steam, and is coming to Switch 2. The game has surpassed five million copies sold on consoles and 28 million copies sold overall.

If you own a pair of headphones in GTA 6, you can even listen to your favorite shows while on foot for the very first time

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rockstar has made some vital changes to the way that you listen to music, access podcasts, and change radio stations in GTA 6. You can even listen to music outside of your vehicles for the first time, so long as you have the necessary headgear purchased and equipped.

Below you'll find a quick rundown of how to listen to music in GTA 6, how to access on-demand podcasts, and where to buy your own headphones to listen to your favorite songs from the GTA 6 soundtrack while you're roaming around the world of Leonida.

There are radios in GTA 6 everywhere. In your safehouse, in whatever vehicles you're driving around, and sometimes you'll find them out in the world too. Thankfully, how to use a radio and change stations in GTA 6 rarely changes.

When you're driving a car you'll want to hold Left on the D-pad to access the radio controls. This is also true for radios in the world, bikes, boats, and planes. Whilst you are holding Left on the D-Pad, you can scroll between all of the radio stations either with L1/LB and R1/RB, or with the right thumbstick. Select the station that you want, stop holding the D-pad button, and it'll start playing. You can also go into this menu and press X/A to turn off the radio entirely.

You can also activate 'On Demand' programming in GTA 6 like podcasts in a similar way. Activate that radio menu again by holding Left on the D-pad, only now you want to press Down with the right thumbstick. This will let you access all of the podcasts which are available to you. You can even press Square/ X on each to scroll between episodes, and then press X/A to play.

Tip: If you actively go into the on-demand section of the radio menu, you can pause the podcast that you're listening to. Head back in here later (regardless of whether you're on foot or back in a vehicle) and it'll sync playback up to where you left off.

Buying a set of headphones allows you to listen to radio and podcasts while outside of a vehicle. To get headphones, open the GTA 6 Index and scroll to the Style tab. In here you're looking for the 'Electronics' option which will display all shops that sell these items, ordered by the one that's closest to your current location. Head over to one of these stores to purchase a pair of headphones or earbuds – these range upwards of $100 for a basic set through to more luxurious models depending on the store, and remember that both Jason and Lucia will need to purchase their own.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Once you have purchased headphones in GTA 6, you'll need to equip them. Hold L1/LB to open your loadout and press R1/RB to navigate to the items tab. The second slot in the wheel is for headgear; navigate to this slot with the right thumbstick and press X to equip your headphones. From there, it's as easy as holding Left on the D-pad to access the radio stations and on-demand podcasts.

If you bought headphones and now can't find them in the menu, it's possible that you have lost them in combat. If you get attacked by the cops or a civilian in the world with headphones equipped, these can get knocked to the ground. Don't forget to pick them back up once you're done brawling, otherwise they will be lost forever!

#3828. Cyberpunk trading sim Probably Stolen is getting three big updates with new starting scenarios - organ trading, junk empires and fine dining

Mucky and disreputable kiosk game Probably Stolen – Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim is getting three big updates over the next few months that add extra starting scenarios, building on the existing wealth of goods, materials, vocations and techs. Those starting scenarios range from peddling human meat to running the finest cyber-frappucino stall this side of Tannhäuser Gate. There are no hard release dates, and the contents of each update may alter, but developers Questing Goose Studio have shared some rough timeframes.

Coming up in mid-December, there's the Junker starting scenario, which I assume is all about trading scrap, rather than being a Prussian nobleman. You'll get a bespoke perk, new items, and the ability to hire, equip and send scavs on expeditions. This update will also include some minor expansions for the Fence and Gunsmith vocations – the latter will be able to flog or otherwise make use of shotgun shells, 25mm grenade rounds and a tier 3 handmade SMG, alongside new armour.

Late January is when you'll "very likely" get the chance to be an Organ Dealer, care of the second major update. "Players will start by buying different organs and fulfilling specific requests, and will later be able to grow or print organs," a Steam blog explains. You'll also be able to filter blood and remove diseases, with different blood types having different value modifiers. How will you get your hands on organs? By sending horrible black market thugs on foraging "expeditions".

Last but not least, the planned April update will add the Street Food Vendor starting scenario. This lets you weave a livelihood around choice beverages and edibles from a range of cultures, supported by updates to the game's Aquaculture and Hydroponics tech. Sounds a lot cheerier than the organ trading racket, but then again, Probably Stolen will doubtless find a way to make it utterly grim. Guests at Sweeney's Cantina know better than to ask what our frappucinos are made of.

Are you playing Probably Stolen? It's been doing better than expected. I was keen on the demo, but my attention was lured away by a truly upsetting game about dogpeople in caves.

#3827. Will a Grand Theft Auto game ever be set outside of America? Rockstar offers a small glimmer of hope

The Grand Theft Auto games have always been synonymous with America; Americana is baked into the crime series' very being. Across its history, there's only ever been one GTA game set outside America: the London-based expansion of the original game.

GTA 6 follows this template, parodying the American state of Florida and the city of Miami. But what about the next game - will the series always be in America? Not necessarily.

In an interview with The Guardian, Rockstar North co-studio boss Rob Nelson propped the proverbial door open a sliver by saying: "Never say never." He then quickly followed that comment with: "But there’s still so much to do in America".

This is a topic Rockstar has responded to before, most notably when company co-founder and long-time GTA writer Dan Houser - who's no longer at Rockstar - discussed why the series always seemed to return to America. He said it was because cities like Miami and New York and Los Angeles are places where extreme juxtapositions exist. They're places where extreme wealth rubs shoulders with extreme poverty, and where organised crime can be found.

There's also something America infamously has that few other countries do, and that's free availability of guns, which is such a core tenet of a GTA experience.

Nevertheless, Obbe Vermeij - a former technical director at Rockstar North - revealed last year that a GTA: Tokyo almost happened. However, it wasn't going to be made by Rockstar but rather an external team in Japan.

While discussing the subject, Vermeij referred to America as "basically the epicenter of Western culture". "Everybody knows the cities, even people who haven't been there," Vermeij said. "They have a mental image of the cities. I'm afraid we're stuck in this loop of about five American cities. Let's just get used to it."

GTA 6 is just days away from its 19th November release on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. Rockstar recently clarified the game runs at 30FPS across all platforms and confirmed that while it's available through Xbox Cloud Gaming, it cannot be streamed to PCs or non-Xbox devices.

AMD landed itself in hot water with gamers a couple of weeks back by saying the quiet part out loud: CEO Dr. Lisa Su announced that it was a "datacentre-first company" in a call with investors, who were likely to want to hear that sorta thing. Yet upon reaching gamers' ears, the news wasn't so well received.

Now, AMD Japan has tried to settle things down by proclaiming "AMD loves gamers."

To be fair, those two statements aren't mutually exclusive. AMD can be datacentre first, and absolutely is, and still claim to care about gaming. Though when supply for key components is tight and prices are rising, we're definitely looking for a little more than kind words at this time.

What makes matters worse is that AMD Japan also added: "AMD values its interactions with gamers above all else."

In Q3, AMD made more than double the cash from its datacentre segment ($8.5 billion) than its client and gaming segment ($3.7 billion)—the latter includes various Ryzen, as well as Radeon, products. Pure gaming revenue was a mere $773 million, and dropping fast, whereas datacentre revenue was up 97%.

So, from a purely business perspective, AMD is undoubtedly all in on datacentres. I don't like to admit it, but it makes sense for a company owned by shareholders to go after the biggest growth market. But all the more reason not to claim an undying love for gamers—it just doesn't pass muster.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

AMD Japan is responding to a tweet from our sister site, Tom's Hardware, who had reported that the company's CEO had attended a store opening for a new Micro Center in Austin, Texas and was handing out autographed graphics cards and swag bags to lucky attendees. So, in that sense, AMD can claim to have helped a handful of gamers directly. An RX 9070 XT signed by Lisa Su may hold its value more than one signed by Jensen Huang.

Nevertheless, the post on X hasn't been too well received. A reader note has been added to note AMD's claim to be a datacentre first company, and the replies are a bit of a dumpster fire.

Truth be told, it's not a good time to claim to care about the gamers, whether there's any truth to the claim or not. From graphics cards to SSDs, we're stuck with extremely high prices, beyond most reasonable budgets, and few exciting product launches to note—except monitors. Thank God for monitors.

#3824. What are we all playing this weekend?

Ah, yes, Saturday. Traditionally a day for relaxing. Why is it then I'm packing, doing last-minute shopping, and going to a wedding all in the space of eight hours? Because, Julian, you are a fool who, as ever, has left everything far too late.

What about the team, though. I imagine they've managed their time much better.

JamesI've got a date with Derelikt, a retro survival-horror FPS with just a dash of immsim keycode hunting. I'm not expecting gee-oh-tee-why material but I do respect any game whose minimum system requirements read, in their entirety, "Sound Card: Toaster Spec".

MarkLast weekend of freedom before I, both cheekily and I assure you temporarily, abandon my PC in order to play a certain game I've been waiting for since I was about 14. I should probably play something strategy-oriented or with extra swanky graphics to get in some more preemptive atonement for my sins. I might end up playing Sleeping Dogs instead.

OllieI want to spend more time in Marathon this weekend. The PvE roguelite-ness of Cryo Archive is intriguing, and I want to see how different the runs can get.

EdwinThis weekend I'm going to shop for a fan heater. I have an unhealthy love of fan heaters. They are my spirit animals. I fancy upgrading to one of those big Dyson things that looks like a mini hyperspace jumpgate, but I assume they're costly both to buy and run.

CallumWith GTA 6 now looming on the horizon, I shall spend this weekend with as few video games as possible. I’ll sit and meditate, like a great warrior prepping for the war to come. Many guides shall be written. Many hours shall be spent looking at virtual guns. Many digital policemen's lives will be taken with big bazookas. But for now, I rest… and probably eat a lot of food.

JeremyThis is the last weekend I must work on our Castlevania walkthrough after almost 50 days of continuous effort. The end is in sight and only then will the morning sun come to vanquish this horrible night.

JulianWhy have I still got too much to do? Because for some reason I decided to start a new BattleTech campaign this week and didn't use my evenings productively crossing items off my to-do list. If I get a free hour (ha!) I'll settling into my mech and cause a ruckus.

#3823. Paradox boss Frederik Wester stepping down after several tumultuous years for the Cities Skylines and Stellaris publisher

Deputy CEO Mattias Lilja taking over role.

Paradox Interactive's Frederik Wester has announced he's stepping down from the role of CEO after a combined decade and a half leading the company. The news follows several tumultuous years for the publisher best known for grand strategy games including Stellaris, Europa Universalis, and Crusader Kings 3.

In a statement announcing the change in leadership, Paradox said Wester had "decided to step down as CEO to continue focusing on the company's long-term development as a member of the Board." Paradox's current deputy CEO, Mattias Lilja, will take over Wester's role from 4th January 2027. Wester is to remain in the position until then in order "to ensure an orderly transition".

"I'm truly grateful to all our engaged players and talented colleagues who contribute to outstanding gaming experiences every day," Wester said of his decision. "They are the ones who made these years amazing. My plan was never to be CEO for life. The goal was to build the foundation before passing the baton on for the next chapter in the company's journey. Since I returned as CEO, we've streamlined our strategy, rebuilt our pipeline and developed our commercial offering. Mattias has had a central role in laying this foundation, and now is the right time to hand over. Given his experience and vision, he is exceptionally well positioned to take the company to its next level."

Wester has twice served as Paradox CEO since joining the company in 2003. His first stint ran from 2009 to 2018, after which he became Paradox's executive chairman of the board. He returned to the CEO role in 2021, and has overseen a troubled period for the company. This has included the embattled development of Vampire: The Masquerade Bloodlines 2 - which finally launched last October after multiple delays, near cancellation, and a switch in developer. Unfortunately the game failed to resonate with critics and audiences, and Paradox announced a 162 percent decline in operating profit earlier this year as a result of its commercial failure.

Wester's most recent watch - which began with an admittance of "inappropriate behaviour" amid a damning report into Paradox's workplace culture - has also seen the high-profile cancellation of Sims competitor Life By You, an indefinite delay for Prison Architect 2 after Paradox parted ways with original developer Double Eleven, and a split with BattleTech studio Harebrained Schemes following the commercial failure of The Lamplighters League. Paradox's Cities Skylines 2 has also been blighted with controversy: after a disastrous launch in 2023, its console release is still yet to emerge, and development is now being handled by a new studio after Paradox split with former developer Colossal Order last year. In 2004, Wester admitted the publisher had "made the wrong calls in several projects".

Despite all this, incoming CEO Mattias Lilja remains buoyant. "Paradox has a unique DNA that has made us one of the greats in deep and engaging strategy and management games," he wrote in a statement announcing his promotion. "Now we’re stepping up the pace: we will make further investments in our core business, push the boundaries of our game design, work even more closely with our loyal players, develop more and better tools and services that benefit both modders and players, and continue to sharpen our ways of working and our organisation, with player value in focus."

Paradox, does of course, have some promising games on its upcoming slate. Alongside continued work on grand strategy stalwarts like Crusader Kings 3, Europa Universalis 5, and Stellaris, next year sees the release of Lego Skylines, and post-apocalyptic grand strategy game Afterworld is also on the way.

The Wanted Level goes up to six now, but it isn't for the faint of heart

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the entirety of my time playing the game for review, I was only able to reach a six-star Wanted level in GTA 6 the one time. That's partially because I was hell bent on maintaining a 'Professional' Criminal Profile in GTA 6, and also because it's really difficult to activate. You have to really be on a bit of a mad one to get this level of heat coming down on you.

If you aren't aware, GTA 6 brought back six stars to the Wanted system. You typically gain heat for doing everything from trespassing to petty crime to big bank robberies, with different numbers of stars indicating the volume of cops (and eventually military) who respond to try and bring you in.

My only six-star encounter in GTA 6 was the result of a firefight with a regular citizen that went awry, the accidental throwing of a grenade at a bunch of cop cars, and then a high-speed pursuit which lasted for well-over 15 minutes and eventually resulted in me hijacking an aeroplane in a desperate attempt to gain some ground. As it turns out, it's only mass destruction and loss of life which will get you six-stars of trouble in GTA 6.

The problem with getting a 6-star wanted level in GTA 6 is that there's actually no way to resolve it. Once you've got that sort of heat on you, the cops and the military will not stop in their pursuit of you. My poor aeroplane lasted just minutes after jets were dispatched to bring me crashing down to Earth.

Interestingly enough, there is a GTA 6 cheat code to raise the wanted level, but no matter how many times I put in the activation code, it would never go above five stars. Which is all to say, the game really is only giving you a 6 star wanted level in GTA 6 when you really deserve it. And then once you've got it… settle in for some pretty outrageous carnage.

#3821. After two weeks of multiplayer downtime, Dark Souls 2 & 3's mysterious server "issue" has been fixed, so it no longer feels so lonely online

Developer FromSoftware has announced that online multiplayer servers for Dark Souls 2 and 3 are back online following a nearly two-week outage.

FromSoftware temporarily disabled multiplayer on 30th October, citing what it called "a server issue". Some speculated this could be related to the recently discovered PHP security bug, which impacted a number of other games.

FromSoftware never specified the exact issue impacting its servers, and today's statement is equally vague. "Regarding the temporary suspension of the game server for Dark Souls 2, and Dark Souls 3, the investigation has been completed and the fix has been applied. The game server and online features are now restored," a notice on Dark Souls' official site reads.

"We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience caused, and thank you for your patience and understanding."

Online servers do more in FromSoftware games than simply facilitating co-op and PvP; they're also responsible for handling messages players leave for each other in-game, as well as the ghostly representations of players who just went through the same area, helping the Dark Souls series' forlorn worlds feel a little less solitary.

This isn't the first time Dark Souls servers have gone offline, either. In 2022, servers for all three games went offline due to a vulnerability that allowed malicious code to run on them. In that instance, it took FromSoftware three months to bring servers back online for some games, and as many as nine months for others.

In other FromSoftware news, the studio recently announced - following months of speculation - it's officially delaying the Switch 2-exclusive The Duskbloods to sometime in 2027.

#3820. Missed something on your first go around The Blood of Dawnwalker? I've got good news, as next week's update adds in new game plus

A big part of the point of The Blood of Dawnwalker is that you're on a fixed time limit. You've got 30 in-game days and nights to try and save your family, and if you don't manage to see everything the game has to offer, well, the game's director is fine with that. But that doesn't matter as much now, as The Blood of Dawnwalker is getting its 1.2 update next week that adds in a new game plus mode.

"If you completed the Epilogue, you can dive right back into Vale Sangora with New Game+!" a post from the devs explains. "Your level, skills, and inventory will carry over; the level cap will be raised to 100; enemies will be balanced and scale uniformly across all regions; and items will have NG+ versions with updated stats." Sounds like your usual new game plus affair! I suppose it is a good opportunity to try out different things compared to your first playthrough, but I'm not exactly aligned with the idea that the timer restriction is too restricting (as some mods have made clear how others feel that way).

In any case, the update goes a tad further than that. If you got the Eclipse Edition of the game, the in-game soundtrack that came with it "will be extended with additional songs from the game." You can expect the soundtrack on streaming services soon, too. While details are slimmer here, there are also some planned balance changes, like updated enemy health pools and how often they use their abilities during combat, and terrain geometry has seen some improvements to allow for "smoother movement during combat and exploration."

Overall, a bit of a smaller update compared to the last one, but one I'm sure will be welcome to some all the same. If you've not had a chance to check the game out yet and still feel on the fence about it, here's some lovely words from Mark's review: "There’s always that sense that something important or unexpected could be lurking around the next corner, to pull you into a quest dripping with depth and intrigue. It works to ensure the more busywork-esque tasks attached to angering Brencis and his Boyars never make Vale Sangora feel home to a string of boring boxes to tick. It’s a vibrant, constantly changing place with a thousand different threads metaphorically criss-crossing just beneath its surface, just as ancient ruins literally criss-cross beneath its swamps, crags, and forests."

"They may come out five years from now, and the world may not care."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It may be hard to notice what with all the Grand Theft Auto 6-ness happening right now, but the games industry has had a very rough last few years. This isn't to say no great games have come out this year. I've actually had a great time, what with Resident Evil Requiem, Onimusha: Way of the Sword, and Big Walk—oh and I've heard that Queen's Domain is rather good also.

But the issue of how big studios are able to balance their budget still stands. “Around content, AAA is under the most amount of threat," former Take-Two CEO, Ben Feder says in an interview with The Game Business. "They’re not big enough to really be platforms on the one hand, and they’re not small enough to really innovate on the other. If you talk to the major publishers, they cannot figure out a way to make a game for less than $300 million, and that to me is just not sustainable."

We now know for sure that GTA 6 is a winner: just look at this review score round up. But there are some worried that replicating this success is nigh impossible for any other studio. As Feder puts it, not everyone can take their "entire development team, putting them in a time capsule, burying them in the ground, and five years later they pop out and say, 'Voila, here it is.'" Most studios simply do not have the capacity or funds to have a team solely working on a project for around a decade.

"Three to five years ago, that was reasonable because we know what they’re building, it’s good IP, they have a niche, and we know what the world’s going to look like when they pop out of the ground," Feder adds. "Today, while they’re underground, on the surface of planet Earth all of this change is happening, not just technologically but also with respect to consumer tastes and expectations. They may come out five years from now, and the world may not care."

Feder goes on to explain that GTA 6 is the exception to this rule as it's able to deliver "escape velocity". I take this to mean the ridiculous amounts of hype and money that surround this game is why it's able to retain this old way of working. "Scale matters there, and you need an enormous amount of capital to do that,” Feder says. "The amount of capital required starts with a 'B' not with an 'M', for sure."

#3817. The Witcher 3 uses gen-AI to enhance Geralt's Polish voice following actor's stroke - "I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically"

"I have great trust ... for the creators of this game."

CD Projekt Red has revealed that it used - and is using - generative AI technology to treat and alter the voice of the Polish actor who portrayed Geralt of Rivia in upcoming Witcher 3 expansion Songs of the Past.

The actor, Jacek Rozenek, has portrayed Geralt of Rivia in all the major Witcher games, meaning his voice has become as synonymous with the role in Poland as Doug Cockle's has for people playing in English. But Rozenek suffered a severe stroke in 2019 that left him temporarily unable to speak, and when he was able to talk and perform again, the tonality and quality of his voice had changed.

It's for these reasons that CD Projekt Red - with Rozenek's consent - employed the help of a company called Respeecher to alter the lines he recorded for The Witcher 3's Songs of the Past expansion using generative-AI technology. As confirmed to Game File, an AI trained on Rozenek's previous Witcher work is retreating his recordings to make them sound more like the Geralt you hear elsewhere in The Witcher 3.

"The point is that this voice should be as close as possible to my voice from 12 years ago," Jacek Rozenek explained. "I have great trust ... for the creators of this game."

Game File heard both treated and untreated recordings of Rozenek's Songs of the Past work, and reported a "significant" difference between them. Rozenek's untreated voice was apparently "deep and gravelly" and "noticeably rougher than his recordings for the original game". But treated, the voice was "far smoother and sounds younger", and closer to the original Witcher 3 Geralt recordings.

This isn't the first time CD Projekt Red has used generative AI for voice recordings in one of its games. The studio worked with Respeecher in 2023 to produce new voiceover lines for Cyberpunk 2077 expansion Phantom Liberty. Viktor Vektor actor Miłogost "Miłek" Reczek passed away in 2021, after the original game was released, and CD Projekt Red didn't want to recast the role. Reczek's sons apparently gave their blessing for their father's voice to be artificially generated.

"I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically with consent and also to do something good," CD Projekt Red localisation producer Mikołaj Szwed told Game File, referring to the Rozenek recordings.

"For future projects, when we consider Geralt is becoming older and has a deeper voice, this is not a problem for us at all. It's more about this specific situation here, where we have both the voice from 12 years ago and from now next to each other, which could kind of take people out of the experience and feel that there is this difference."

The third Witcher 3 expansion, Songs of the Past, releases at some point next year, an unprecedented 12 years after the original game launched. It adds an entirely new region, Letten, and centres its main story around Geralt's missing bardic bestie Dandelion, whose family lives there.

In preparation for the expansion, a remastered version of The Witcher 3 was released a couple of months ago, overhauling the old role-playing adventure and bringing its baseline presentation more in line with what we'd expect from a modern game; it also overhauled some animations and enemy behaviours and reworked skill trees. For that reason, old-gen consoles PS4 and Xbox One won't receive the Songs of the Past expansion, despite The Witcher 3 being available on them.

#3816. From 2D to 3D and back to 2D again, the original platforming classic Super Meat Boy returns with a slick remaster complete with new levels and too many old saws

Earlier this year in a bit of a shakeup for the fleshiest kid in town, Super Meat Boy entered into a new dimension in the aptly named Super Meat Boy 3D. I've not played it but it seems like a good take on the format. Clearly, though, sometimes you just need to play the hits, as a new release of the original game is on the way in the form of Super Meat Boy Again+, a remaster with updated graphics, levels and plenty more.

What is there is very clearly Super Meat Boy, uh, again, just with a big new lick of paint. There is probably some kind of joke to be made about it being DLSS yassified, but I'm too tired to think of one, so, you get the point. But it does look pretty good! I do kind of miss the Flash game aesthetic, I think there's a real charm to the sort of visual design sensibilities you'd find from that era, but this remaster certainly ain't ugly at least. Apparently it's not just the art that's new, as there's also new music, cutscenes, secrets and "stuff."

If the animated sequences featured in the trailer, which you can have a gander at above, are included in the final game that'll be a treat to watch too, as I think they better capture the Newgrounds pseudo sub-genre of animation than the graphical overhaul. It sounds like they will be looking at the Steam page, so, a treat to look forward to while committing an act of masochism by playing it!

There's no release date attached to this remaster, so we'll all just have to sit tight for an update there. The original is still listed on Steam, but if you fancy as big a dose of nostalgia as the trailer is trying to present to you, you could always go play the original, plain old regular Meat Boy. It's playable right on Newgrounds thanks to the Flash emulator Ruffle and works like a dream! Or if you're happy to wait, you could always wishlist the new one on Steam.

#3814. Firaxis Games lays off a third of staff

Firaxis Games, the 2K-owned studio behind the Civilization and XCOM series, has laid off around 60 people today, or about a third of its staff, according to a Bloomberg report citing people familiar with the matter.

Studio head Heather Hazen will depart as part of the cuts, a 2K spokesperson confirmed.

“Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength—designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years,” the spokesperson said.

They continued, “As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis.”

Bloomberg reports that Firaxis Games has been working on a new XCOM game that has faced development struggles and missed a significant milestone over the summer. Development will continue, but may face a shakeup as a result of the layoffs.

#3813. After days of controversy, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned

Nvidia's founder and CEO Jensen Huang has resigned from his position as leader of one of the most valuable companies in the world.

After days mired in controversy, which began amid reports of Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy, Nvidia has announced Huang's resignation as company president, chief executive officer, and board member, effective immediately. Finance chief Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO and will remain in the position until a permanent CEO is chosen.

"Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position," Harvey Jones, chair of Nvidia's board of directors wrote in a statement accompanying the news. "She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing Nvidia's strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption."

Kress, in the same announcement, says she intends to build on the foundation laid by Huang over the past 33 years, and "continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead." Perhaps unsurprisingly, there's no mention of gaming graphics cards in there.

Nvidia's announcement ends by thanking Huang for his time at the company: "Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry."

Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to decide whether to remove Huang amid allegations he had participated in a second affair, this time with a subordinate, following reports of his alleged affair with a Chinese spy. That initial incident prompted a company-wide apology from Huang and an independent investigation exploring whether he'd been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort".

Nvidia will likely remain under increased scrutiny moving forward. There are particular concerns around the company's chips being imported to China despite trade bans.

#3812. Congratulations to people who feel mean shooting random NPCs, because GTA 6 tries "to provide mechanisms that encourage" empathy

When you think about GTA as a series, the first thing that probably comes to mind is driving through crowds of people, gunning down whoever you like, just generally doing crime without any care in the world. I wouldn't exactly call it an empathy game, not to say that other games are any better at such a thing anyway. But with GTA 6 out, crikey, next bloody week, a new interview has gone up with co-studio head Rob Nelson where he shared that you have a bit more space to be empathetic compared to previous entries.

"Crime is a fundamental part of GTA - at least up until now, it has been," Nelson told The Guardian (via @GameRoll_, ta IGN) in a new interview. "We're trying to make sure we're not punishing people for playing the game they are used to … [but] your actions will have some effect on how the game plays out." When asked about whether this will be the first GTA game to encourage people to be empathetic, Nelson responded, "I would say so. I would say that it's a product of the story we're trying to tell. We've tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to."

I am deeply curious as to what those mechanics may be, given that most of what we've seen so far is pretty relegated to shootin', lootin' and a bit of smoochin'. If you steal a car, is there an NPC that loses their job because of it? Can you repair the harm you caused through that action? I'm sure hardly anyone else that's vibrating through their skin in excitement for almost having the game in their fingertips will be asking such questions, I'm just often wary of empathy mechanics in games.

In any case, doesn't matter all that much for us PC lot just yet, especially because Rockstar are preparing themselves both legally and technically to tackle pirated copies of the game. Rockstar will obviously be quite busy at the moment too, not just because of that whole launching a game thing, but because UK-based workers will be voting to unionise as we speak. If formed, it could be 1600 members strong, which would make it the biggest games union in the UK. Solidarity with all the workers as the voting process continues. I hope you get the result you deserve.

#3810. As low-effort AI slop continues to flood Steam, yet more developers announce game delays caused by Valve's growing approval backlog

"There's no outcome of this that allows Valve neutrality on AI".

More indie developers say they've been forced to delay the impending release of their games as a result of Steam's growing approvals backlog - a relatively recent problem that's believed to stem from an influx of AI slop on the platform.

Earlier this month, developers began complaining about delays to Valve's approval process, which was extending the time it took to get their games published on Steam. Valve responded, explaining approval times could now take up to 12 days, due to the number of submissions it was having to re-review. One week on, the situation doesn't seem to have improved.

New turn-based tower defence game Australia Did It: End-of-the-World Railway Defense Business, co-developed by acclaimed indie designer Rami Ismail and Aesthetician Labs, was previously set for release on 10th November. Unfortunately, the game has now been delayed while the wait continues for Valve to review the latest build.

"We're still waiting for Steam to give us the final greenlight and finish their build review process," publisher Mystic Forge wrote on the Steam forums. "We have been stuck waiting for it for a few weeks now and unfortunately we just don't know when they will get around to reviewing it at this point."

Speaking to Eurogamer, Ismail added that Australia Did It has been in Steam's approval queue for much longer than he's used to: "We've been in the queue since 20th October, failed over a minor controller input issue on 5th November (which we resolved the same day), and we've been waiting again since with no meaningful response from Valve despite follow-ups."

"I'm used to hold-and-wait patterns on console," Ismail continued, "but Steam has historically been much more snappy - 10-14 days pre-launch was usually enough to fail twice and still ship on time," he added.

Amazing Slot Survivor (A.S.S.), the debut title from TwoMenGames, is facing similar issues, and has had to retract its release date announcement after being stuck in Steam's approval queue. Amazing Slot Survivor, which adds a slot machine spin to the bullet heaven auto-shooting genre, was initially set for release on 13th November.

"Steam's review process for the release is taking longer than we expected," TwoMenGames wrote in a message on Steam. "We know many of you have been counting on the schedule we announced earlier, and we are very sorry to bring you this [postponement] news instead of the good news you were hoping for." Amazing Slot Survivor's demo, which was previously set to disappear with the game's full release, has returned to Steam until the developer announces a new launch date.

These are far from the only examples, and a cursory look on social media reveals many more indie games are affected by the problem, including the likes of Bottled by Bears, and Food Devils.

Valve recently attempted to address the delays its facing by introducing stricter submission guidelines designed to stop the lowest-effort games, such as those vibe-coded entirely with gen-AI, from joining its approval queue. However, Ismail doesn't think that's good enough.

"I am concerned that Valve trying to avoid taking a political position on AI is forcing them into choices that will inevitably be worse for developers," he told Eurogamer. "If sloppers can submit several game clones a day through automated systems, the only way for Valve to stem the tide of games damaging genuine developers' work is to put constraints on game distribution, increase fees, or make the process more complicated.

"In the 'open market' Valve seems to so adore, they're going to be the ones carrying the costs for moderation, so I don't think they'll like the open market on this - but there's no outcome of this that allows Valve neutrality on AI and not do things that will ultimately make life worse for genuine developers," he added.

#3808. Rasen, out in early access now, is a PvP focused take on Dark Souls that borrows one of fighting games' best techy tricks

The idea of Dark Souls PvP has always scared me a tad. You can replace Dark Souls with Bloodborne or Elden Ring, I've typically just been a coward when it comes to the idea of fighting another, real person. They're probably going to be better than me! I don't use tactics in Souls games, I use brute force until I get my way! That being said, I do have to admit I quite like the look of Rasen, a game that is essentially just the PvP component of Dark Souls (or PvE if you just want to take on some computer-controlled enemies) that just launched into early access.

To say that it is just straight up Dark Souls combat would be unfair, from the looks of things. For one, it looks more like it leans a tad towards Sekiro with a blades-only kind of affair, whether that be big or small. And blades a plenty they have, ranging from your classic sword, to scythes, to halberds and all sorts. It's a much flashier looking affair too, with fancy slashing effects that seem to buff moves and a pace that seems much faster than Souls games tend to be.

You can take part in matches with up to eight people, which presumably extends to AI (not that kind) enemies too, in "atmospheric duels, clashes, deathmatches and more." It looks neat! And best of all, unusually for a 3D arena fighter, it has rollback netcode. For those unfamiliar, and to try and explain it simply, this is essentially a bit of tech you'll find in predominantly 2D fighting games that predicts every possible input you could make in a given moment, helping to reduce lag time and allow for tighter matches (and less rage quitting).

That's a bit harder to do in a 3D environment given that you have a lot more options at your disposal when it comes to movement, so if it works that's some impressive stuff! And we could all quite easily find out together, as a demo for Rasen is available to try out. Or, alternatively, you can just pick it up whole hog on Steam right now, as it's available in early access.

Money in GTA 6 is made most quickly through crime, as you might expect.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You can farm and make money quick in GTA 6 in a variety of different ways, and the options available to you are going to change chapter by chapter as you work through the main story. Different and more lucrative opportunities will present themselves as Jason and Lucia's crime spree across Leonida continues, but there are some basics you'll want to wrap your head around as you start your journey.

Once you understand how to manage your money in GTA 6, you'll naturally want to start increasing your Personal Cash and BuckMe Checking Account reserves – especially if you feel a desire to save for your family in GTA 6. Making money can be done in numerous ways, some of which are more effective or efficient than others.

There are several methods to farm money fast in Grand Theft Auto 6, all of which I'll lay out below and go into more detail on further down:

As is perhaps to be expected, risk through crime is the best way to make cash fast in GTA 6, though obviously there's a certain amount of nuance to that idea. It means that the best thing you can do to farm cash is work out an efficient crime spree, though keep in mind that this might have serious implications for your criminal profile.

The easiest way to make a little pocket cash in GTA 6 is to mug random civilians and stick up convenience stores. Robbing people on the street can be activated by aiming your unholstered weapon at a person and pressing Triangle / Y to demand their valuables. Holding up cashiers in stores, restaurants, and gas stations works much in the same way: aim your weapon at the staff and press Square / X to demand cash from the register.

Tip: Once you have the money to attach a winch to your vehicle at a Mod Shop, you can also steal ATM machines in GTA 6.

Once you've learned how to steal cars in GTA 6, you'll want to start targeting them to make some decent money. Whether you've broken into the vehicle, or hijacked one from somebody on the street by aiming your weapon at the driver, cars in good condition can then be sold at certain businesses and contacts. In Chapter 2 you'll gain access to Moses' auto shop in GTA 6 which is a great way to make some cash, although you can also sell vehicles at any of the GTA 6 Pay 'n' Spray locations too.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Tip: Check the GTA 6 index as you progress through the game to find specific fences who will take cars with some heat on them. Multiple will unlock, looking for different classes of car, in different chapters.

Robberies are the best way to make fast money in GTA 6. Using the Robberies section of the map index is a great way to identify high-yield opportunities and a list of known illegal operations. When you hover over the location of a gang hideout, Smash 'n' Grab location, Bank, or Payday Loan vendor the summary will denote what the potential score is and any key valuables which may be recovered. Just remember, the bigger the score, the more dangerous it is likely to be.

Tip: Larger robbery and Illegal Operations are going to be easier to survive if you bring your partner with you for support, so don't forget to learn how to switch characters in GTA 6.

GTA 6 missions will typically earn you a little bit of money, so completing story objectives is a great way to keep your checking account filled. You can also earn cash by participating in activities at bars like pool, as well as a whole host of other racing opportunities which are spread across the map. You'll discover more of these locations and racing spots as you progress through the story, but don't forget to check in at local motels and hotels to see if they have any pamphlets or town maps which can be observed that can put local spots directly onto your map.

Tip: You will gain access to different vehicle, narcotics, and jewellery fences in GTA 6 as you progress through Chapter 1-4 of the main story.

A stable 30 fps on RDNA 2 hardware with a game this stunning is promising.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

From what we're already seeing of Grand Theft Auto 6 on console, it's boding very well for a future PC release. It might only be targeting 30 fps on console, but with how stable that is and with the graphics looking so stunning on older PS5/PS5 Pro hardware, I've got high hopes for how it might run on our gaming PCs.

Digital Foundry (DF) has taken one for the team here by doing some performance testing on an inferior platform (cheap shot, I'm sorry). And judging from the screenshots, videos, and frame rate analysis so far, GTA 6 looks very much next-gen in terms of scale, scope, and fidelity.

We're talking fine detail on the local scale combined with open, bustling sight lines to the horizon, depending on your vantage point. All very noticeably saturated by incredible ray traced lighting, and running at a stable 30 fps on the PS5 Pro.

It's hard to describe how fantastic GTA looks. It does seem like a new era for open world games.

What particularly impresses me, judging from DF's gameplay and graphics shots, is how seamlessly fine detail combines with great lighting and breaks into long distance views.

One minute you're inside a bustling store, with incredibly realistic ambient lighting and reflections thanks to the ray tracing implementation (plus ray traced shadows on the PS5 Pro), admiring the stranded hair on all the NPCs and the little touches such as drinks actually draining in the bottle you drink from.

The next, you can be looking across the entire city without losing any noticeable detail. This seamlessness does make it seem like a real, lively world.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

A large part of this immersion seems to come from the lighting. You're getting full ray traced global illumination, apparently at 1440p resolution which, on the PS5 Pro, reportedly looks more like 4K (and on the base PS5 apparently looks like it might be 1440p upscaled). The PS5 (non-Pro) version looks a little more blurry and lacks the level of shadow definition, but for the most part both versions look great. At least as far as I can tell from DF's footage, anyway.

All of the above is only good news if it runs well, and thankfully on this front it looks like it does. Yes, we're only talking 30 fps, but on the PS5 Pro version, at least, that's a very stable 30 fps. DF says there wasn't a single noticeable stutter or drop in over 50 hours of gameplay, and it's only when you start blowing up cars on the street that you get brief drops down to as low as 24 fps.

The PS5 (non-Pro) is different, struggling to consistently maintain 30 fps even when just driving around the city. But that console has significantly worse hardware compared to the Pro, so it's to be expected—the GPU in the PS5 has just 36 compute units (CUs) compared to the PS5 Pro's 60.

As far as playing GTA 6 on PC is concerned, I think this means we can be hopeful. The PS5 Pro's AMD GPU does have some RDNA 3/4 features, but for the most part it's an RDNA 2 chip. RDNA 2 graphics cards for PC are Radeon RX 6000-series ones. So, even with an older PC using a graphics card that is two generations old, it's possible you'll be able to get the gorgeous graphics you see on the PS5 Pro at a stable 30 fps.

At what settings? Well, that remains to be seen. But considering we'll almost certainly get some more customisation options over on PC, we should be able to eke out as much performance as we can from it, tailored to our hardware.

If you have a newer PC with a newer graphics card, I'd be hoping for 60 fps+ performance, and for that to be stable. The RX 9070 XT, for instance, should outperform a PS5 Pro considerably, despite only having a handful of extra CUs, thanks to the much newer architecture a higher power limit.

Particularly promising is just how stable that 30 fps seems to be on the PS5 Pro. People often think about the average, but don't consider frame pacing and 1% lows. On those fronts, GTA 6 seems very well optimised.

Our Chris has spent 100 hours with the Playstation 5 version of GTA 6, and has come away with some very positive impressions. Here's hoping the PC release lives up to the hype, and that those of us on older rigs might be able to get in on the action without too many pricey upgrades.

Eventually, he gave up the ruthless mercenary life to join the world's #1 PC Gaming site full-time. It's definitely not an ego thing, he assures us.

Calame, a single-player isometric strategy RPG that “blends deep, classic strategy with innovative reality-shifting gameplay,” will launch for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series, and PC via Steam in February 2027, developer Nextale Games announced. A demo is currently available for PC.

Here is an overview of the game, via Nextale:

In the Shadow of the King of Light, History is Written by the Survivors

In Westalia, renown is more than just a story—it is a weapon of mass destruction. When belief in a legend grows strong enough, it can physically reshape the battlefield or devour those who wield it. To overthrow the tyrannical King of Light, the Rebellion must learn to harness this divine force without becoming the very monsters they fight. But how do you save a kingdom when you are tearing yourselves apart?

An uneasy alliance forms the core of the Rebellion. On one side, Kenmare fights for the freedom of the people; on the other, the Panthers fight to reclaim the throne. While their alliance is a matter of sheer survival, their visions for the future are utterly irreconcilable—and you are the one chosen to lead them.

A New Kind of Tactics That Rewrites the Battlefield Itself

In the finest tradition of genre classics, Calame delivers demanding, handcrafted, grid-based combat where positioning, unit facing and class synergies are the keys to survival. Players can customize their army utilizing a diverse roster of melee specialists, ranged fighters, mages and support classes to trigger devastating party combinations.

However, Calame breaks the tactical mold with its groundbreaking “Correction” feature—an innovative new strategy mechanic allowing you to rewrite and manipulate the battlefield mid-combat, turning the terrain itself into a dynamic weapon!

Beyond the battlefield, Calame features deep progression systems including RPG leveling, skill unlocks, and legendary gear collection. Your journey is heavily defined by a reactive choice system. Decisions made at camp and during narrative events directly alter the Rebellion’s political alignment, unlocking powerful passive traits that permanently reshape your squad’s playstyle, faction relationships and the unfolding story.

#3804. World of Warcraft: Forever players in Australia and New Zealand are struggling to get sunlight, and not for the usual MMO reasons

World of Warcraft: Forever players are having a blast in the new MMO, but not everyone is basking in the rays of its successful launch. Players located in Australia, New Zealand, and other Oceania countries are having a bit of a sunlight problem.

But it's not that too much time behind the computer is keeping WoW players on the other side of the globe away from their precious Vitamin D. Rather, it's in-game sunlight that's scarce for our Oceania friends.

World of Warcraft: Forever, if you didn't already known, has a lovely in-game day/night cycle that aligns with your server clock rather than your local time. So, for a British player, the server time is one hour ahead of GMT. That means if I play during the day I see the sun hanging over Azeroth, and if I do a late night MMO session it's replaced by the moon.

However, while Oceania players can access a data centre in Australia that allows for a solid connection to WoW, they still share the same mega-servers with North Americans. That mega-server is aligned with North American time, differing drastically from Oceania time zones. In other words, for World of Warcraft: Forever players in Oceania, day is night and night is day. And they've had enough!

Reddit user Playful_Artichoke981 has been at the forefront of requests asking Blizzard to address the problem , though they're far from alone. Currently, Oceania players see full daylight in-game from around midnight to 6am in the morning, which obviously is far from normal gaming hours for the majority of players in the region.

"We don't hate the nighttime. We just want variety," writes Playful_Artichoke981. "We don't want to have to compromise our sleep schedules to experience this game in all its glory." Another user, cuddlegoop, echoes the sentiment: "I am totally fine with my day/night changing when I join an NA party. Just let me see the sun! I was up late last night and the view over the bay at Shadowfan Keep in the dawn was so beautiful I want to see stuff like that more often."

Eurogamer has contacted Blizzard to ask if it has plans to address the issue, but we've not received a response at the time of writing.

World of Warcraft: Forever is proving exceptionally popular, breaking records as the biggest launch in the series' history. And based on what I've played this week, it's looking to be a brilliant MMO that's well worth jumping into, if you have the time.

#3803. Forage and fight for ingredients in a magical 1960s Italy and whip up some tasty meals Cooking Mama style in The Snackbar at the End of the World

If a game is about cooking, at minimum I'll have to give it a quick testspin. Outside of this whole writing about video games thing, my other lot in life is soul bound to food, so I'm always curious to see how the two can be mixed together. And earlier this week, The Snackbar at the End of the World was revealed, a wonderfully cartoonish action-adventure game set in a magical, slightly post-apocalyptic version of 1960s Italy where you go out and forage for ingredients while fending off monstrous crops before turning them into tasty meals back in your struggling restaurant.

First up, I just have to gush over the artstyle a bit. The whole game is hand-drawn with a colourful, comic book look that has an impressive sense of depth to it. It gives off a deep love of Italian architecture and landscapes, and that admiration clearly extends to the food too. Once you've gotten the ingredients you need, you then, loosely in the vein of Cooking Mama, prepare them and make various classic Italian dishes by performing some quick minigames. Simple, but charming! The rest of the time you're off killing some ghoulies that look like mutated fruit and veggies, with the occasional fungus-possessed hog and, uh, haunted statues? I think?

I'm also quite pleased about two points made on the game's Steam page. First is the content description: "This game features cartoon violence, sensitive political themes set in a fictional world, and depictions of an oppressive government committing crimes against its citizens." There is clearly a romantic quality to the game and I'd be worried if it didn't acknowledge any of the political context of the decades preceding.

The other line reads, "Every sound effect, musical note, design decision, and line of code is human-made. Because this game is about human relationships and delicious food – and that’s not a story we would ever trust AI to tell." Thank the lord! Right now there's no release date attached to The Snackbar at the End of the World, unsurprising given it was only announced this week. But while we all wait for a date, you could perhaps join me in throwing it a wishlist on Steam.

Keeping track of your favorite cars in GTA 6 is one of the most important things that you need to learn how to do

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With over 157 cars and 29 types of bikes available throughout Leonida, understanding how vehicle ownership works in GTA 6 is crucial. Managing the Personal Vehicles of Jason and Lucia is a major priority as they'll be your main mode of transportation around the world.

GTA 6 also handles unowned vehicles, destroyed vehicles, and impounded vehicles in slightly different ways, and the same goes for storing any of your favorites too. So for all things Personal Vehicle-related this car ownership guide will get you up to speed quickly on how vehicles work in GTA 6.

A Personal Vehicle in GTA 6 is the car you are legally registered to ride. Both Jason and Lucia can have their own personal vehicle to call their own, but first they need to be registered (which can be costly, depending on the make and model of the car or bike).

The benefit of investing in a personal vehicle in GTA 6 is that they can always be recovered via the ScooterBros app on your phone if they are lost or destroyed. You're also able to manage your loadout in GTA 6 from the trunk of these vehicles, change your outfit to lower Appearance heat, and store key items such as stash bags and any spoils from hunting trips.

Helpfully, the location of your personal vehicle is always marked on the map. Just open up the GTA 6 Index and scroll to the Personal tab, which is where you'll find your car.

Businesses such as Pay 'n' Sprays (as well as key contacts, once you've unlocked the relevant GTA 6 mission) will register an unowned vehicle as your personal vehicle for a fee. This can be pretty costly, depending on the make and model of the vehicle – and you won't be able to register a vehicle with a standard or advanced tracker until you've progressed far enough in the story.

Locate a local Pay 'n' Spray by heading to the Vehicles section of the map index, and drive the vehicle you want to register over there. Once you're inside, you'll see the option to register the vehicle and the associated cost.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

It's worth noting that while Jason and Lucia can each have their own personal vehicle at any one time, you can register additional cars and bikes in their names once you purchase new garages. So long as you have the space to store them, you can register the vehicle – and you can summon any registered vehicle whenever you want via the ScooterBros app, a service which will deliver the owned car you want and return the one you don't to storage for a fee.

So long as you have the necessary equipment, you can steal pretty much any car that you want to. The last unowned vehicle you drop will be marked on the map under the Personal section of the map index, but unlike Personal Vehicles they can't be recovered if they get destroyed.

So, how do you keep an unowned vehicle safe? Beyond paying the price to register it as a personal vehicle, you have two ways to keep an unowned vehicle around. The first is to set it down in a parking space outside of your safehouse, if available. The other is to store it safely in a garage.

If your vehicle takes enough damage (and you can't find somewhere to repair your car in GTA) then it will eventually become undriveable. If this happens to your Personal Vehicle, it can be recovered via the ScooterBros app for a fee. If this happens to an Unowned Vehicle, not only will it be permanently destroyed but you'll also lose access to anything that was stored in its trunk.

Sometimes the smartest way to lose your Wanted Level in GTA 6 is to dump your vehicle. This will clear your Vehicle Heat and give you a better chance of escaping, but it will most likely result in the cops impounding it. This will also happen if you're Wasted or Busted by the cops while driving your Personal Vehicle.

For a significant fee, you can request the ScooterBros services to recover your ride from the impound lot for you, but this may result in the loss of any stash bags you had hidden in your trunk. If you want a better chance of getting your stuff back, check the Personal section of the map index to see where your vehicle is being held, and then attempt to steal your vehicle back or check nearby cop cars to see if you can recover your loot if they have already removed it from your trunk.

#3801. Xbox boss seemingly champions gen-AI development as she celebrates 25 years of Xbox: "A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers"

Xbox leader Asha Sharma has alluded to harnessing the power of generative AI when making games, in a memo published this afternoon.

The memo, titled 25 years of Xbox, charts the growth of Microsoft from small beginnings through to the thousands-strong company it is today. But it's Sharma's comments at the end of the memo that are of particular interest.

While talking about what the next 25 years could bring, Sharma lamented that "too many ideas never become games" and that "too many games fall short of what their creators imagined". "For decades, this has been the unavoidable tradeoff of ambition," she wrote. "We must change this."

Sharma continued: "Throughout human history, the scale of what we could create was determined by the people, capital, and resources we could command. That relationship is beginning to break. A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations. A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars. And our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today's games as Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 is from its first entry in 1982."

There is no explicit mention of generative AI here, but the language is suggestive - "a single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations". Furthermore, Asha's memo follows last month's announcement of an Xbox Labs initiative that also sounded like it was based around generative AI, despite avoiding the phrase specifically.

This isn't a surprise, of course. Microsoft as a wider company is all-in on generative AI, with Copilot, and Sharma's background at Microsoft is in AI. But it's an area she's avoided speaking too enthusiastically about since her hiring as Xbox boss earlier this year. At the time, Sharma said she has "no tolerance for bad AI", and there's been such a lot else going on in the months since - including wide-ranging restructuring resulting in the loss of thousands of Xbox jobs - that the topic of generative AI has fallen into the background. Perhaps now we're seeing the sprouting seeds of it.
