#3676. World of Warcraft: Forever isn't mere nostalgia bait - it's rebuilding the MMO social architecture that Blizzard spent years dismantling

And when I fall in love, will it be (WoW) Forever?

I don't play video games regularly anymore. Not because I've lost interest in them, but because I no longer make the time, the premium on which has seemed to exponentiate with age. I realised, however, in 2019 that I was a kind of sleeper agent: whenever I heard the opening notes of Legends of Azeroth, the original World of Warcraft login screen music, I would feel the reactivation of a latent part of my mind laid down when I was 10 years old. And so, like a form of possession, whenever Blizzard announces a new legacy iteration of the original WoW, no downpayment in time nor money is too great to prevent me from returning.

Here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019. Once more I set foot on Durotar, to spend as much time as I can levelling up a new Orc Warrior before I am forcibly unplugged by either my boss or, more likely, my wife, and so far it's been a welcome return to some of the frictional - but more involving and consequential - socialising that WoW's decades of updates had previously sanded down.

My relationship with Azeroth began in 2007, when I was ten years old. As soon as I inserted the CD-ROM, I knew that I was going to have to vastly increase my timeshare on the family desktop. For the next six years, school attendance, sleep, and quality family time suffered immensely as I battled to balance my new parallel existence as a member of the Orcish Horde.

It's unremarkable now, but the fact that characters created at WoW's launch are now 22 years old and can still be played in the latest iteration of the game would have been almost inconceivable to many developers at the turn of the century. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the video game industry was overwhelmingly organised around discrete releases expected to have relatively short lives. For most games, commercial success was concentrated in a brief period surrounding their launch, after which sales declined and eventually ceased. WoW's extraordinary success, and exceedingly long half-life, demonstrated the commercial possibilities and durability of a different model: an evolving, immersive digital environment that players paid to inhabit, year after year. Rather than simply purchasing a finished product, players entered a world that would continue to grow around them. New players, after buying the game (and then its subsequent expansions) and paying for a subscription, could begin their adventures in the same world as those who had been there from the beginning, making their way through its ever-expanding geography and history.

The persistence of Azeroth has been the main driver of its abiding allure for me. I have returned to the game time after time, often just to be enveloped in an audiovisual environment that I know so intimately, and which was so formative in my life. But as the WoW universe was continually developed, the game became increasingly unrecognisable from the version I skipped school to play on Windows XP.

What I wanted from the game had also changed. In a turn that would have been completely anathema to my teenage self, I no longer cared about reaching the endgame or having the most competitive character. I stopped caring about the latest raiding content or PvP rankings. Instead, the elements of the game I had once feverishly tried to skip over, like levelling, professions and story, became, ironically, the only parts of the game that I yearned for.

As time unspooled, WoW naturally needed updates to stay fresh. This meant overhauling many of the unwieldy elements of its original design. Much of this was described as 'streamlining' the player experience, making the game less tedious by reducing downtime and, most critically, reliance on other players.

The original Azeroth emulated the real world in ways that few contemporary games do. Firstly, it was openly unbalanced, with some classes vastly stronger than others, some of which were borderline unplayable. Secondly, it required extraordinary amounts of patience and downtime to navigate. Most importantly, though, it required collaboration with others to get the most out of it. In order to access the latest content, players would have to self-organise into specifically composed groups as big as 40 players large, and schedule lengthy chunks of time each week to make progress.

Over time, much of the original social architecture that forced player collaboration was stripped from the game. Adventurers no longer needed to search for and group up with other players from their own server to complete rewarding content. Automated matchmaking systems increasingly did the work for them.

I remember many late nights when I was prevented from doing something quite modest because there were simply not enough players online, or not enough of the right classes. With my ambitions frustrated, I would often have no choice but to log off and try again in the morning. These frustrations were, I only learnt in retrospect, an important byproduct of inhabiting a world that did not exist solely for my benefit. Other people had their own schedules, priorities and ambitions, and my experience of the game depended on those contingencies.

The changes to WoW followed the trajectory of the wider online gaming industry, where players could increasingly be matched instantly with others at any time of day. These were changes that genuinely respected players' time, but the texture and immersion of the game world paid a hefty price. In making the game more convenient, Blizzard had also made it less necessary, and in some respects less possible, to participate in the social world that had once made Azeroth feel so alive.

It became increasingly clear that there was a subset of players, like me, who weren't interested in seeing an old dog learn new tricks, and just wanted to spend time with the old girl we'd raised from a pup. Even if she did walk slowly, and was a bit blind.

As the years went on, many players moved on with their lives, even if they continued to carry some indelible residue of Azeroth with them. Others created unofficial instances of the original game, known as private servers, and relived those infant years with a knowledge of the world that they could scarcely have imagined possessing when they first entered it. As these servers became increasingly popular, Blizzard, originally very reluctant, eventually launched Classic in 2019, an official revival of the game in something approaching its original 2004 form. Since then, legacy versions of WoW have become popular enough to exist alongside the modern game as a major branch of the franchise.

Re-releasing these legacy versions has been a considerable commercial success. But it also exposed a problem with the project of preservation. The original game, because it is so timeworn, has effectively been 'solved.' Players know almost everything about it, including its most obscure idiosyncrasies, and have found ingenious ways of exploiting them. The uncertainty that once made Azeroth feel so vast and mysterious has been replaced by an extraordinary collective expertise. When new content was added to the game, even the best guilds would spend weeks making no progress. During those early years, players at Azeroth's frontiers had to innovate to find creative ways of tackling novel and seemingly intractable problems.

There are clear limits to simulating a turning back of the clock. Players like me slowly realised that we didn't simply want to return to an earlier, simpler period in Azeroth. We wanted something impossible. Like the characters in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, we wanted to forget what we already knew so that we might experience our birth in Azeroth for the first time all over again.

WoW: Forever is an attempt to solve this problem. Like Old School RuneScape, Forever's undeniable forerunner and a considerable success in its own right, it is an expanded re-release of the original game that imagines an alternate future for Azeroth: one in which the game continues to evolve without abandoning the original texture and mechanics, and one that preserves the social architecture that made it so enriching in the first place.

As I write this, my Orc Warrior is sitting at a Campfire, a new mechanic that allows players to establish communal campsites and contribute profession-specific items that confer temporary bonuses to themselves and others. To receive a benefit from Campfires, adventurers are forced to sit together, a deliberate attempt from Blizzard to encourage interactions between players. It is too early to tell how effective this socialising mechanism will be in the long run, but nearly everyone in my experience so far has been eager to shoot the breeze together. I have already shared a number of conversations with other players, most of whom are thirty- or forty-somethings on a similar nostalgia quest as me.

I am playing the game on a laptop using a trackpad, caring very little about efficient or optimal progression. Although I suspect a substantial proportion of the player base shares my approach, not everyone has approached the game so casually. At least five players have already reached maximum level, and many others will have meticulously theory-crafted plans designed to skip straight to the endgame. This is a good thing, and the game should be able to support players with different goals. It's important that the game rewards time and effort, but I hope that the modest amount of time I am able to commit will allow me to feel like I am on my own meaningful adventure, and not a weak player who is trailing behind.

Many in the community have come to believe, perhaps wishfully, that Forever might escape the trap of vertical progression, in which each new wave of content supersedes and renders older content redundant. Instead, the promise of horizontal progression, where new content expands the range of meaningful activities and rewards available without continually raising the ceiling of character power, has been latched on to by members of the community, even though Blizzard's messaging in this regard has not been totally clear.

For players like me, the appeal of horizontal progression is that Azeroth might once again become a place to inhabit, rather than a race to finish. I want to be able to wander off, pursue some obscure profession, or spend an evening doing very little of consequence without feeling that the rest of the world has left me behind. I know I don't have the time to commit to the endgame hamster wheel, and whether Forever will produce a gameworld that meaningfully accommodates players with such different ambitions remains to be seen. But for now, at least, it feels good to be home.

Spoiler alert! This story discusses the Live Shows' Y2K Week on The Voice Season 30, which aired November 16. Episodes are available to stream the day after they air with a Peacock subscription.

The Voice Live Shows are in full swing on the 2026 TV schedule, and have been narrowing down Season 30’s incredible talent to the Top 10. In the latest episode of NBC’s long-running singing competition, they continued to pay tribute to the hits of the late ‘90s and early 2000s with Part 2 of Y2K Week with Team Riley and Team Kelly. From the Goo Goo Dolls hit “Iris” to The Chicks’ tune “Cowboy Take Me Away” to Keane’s indie rock track “Somewhere Only We Know,” there was a blend of musical genres that traveled all over the map and gave a glimpse into how challenging it will be to continue to cut singers, moving ever closer to the winning coach and star. I need to talk about the country music.

While veteran coach Kelly Clarkson knows firsthand what it takes to win, having taken the title four times in nine seasons, including during her first season as a coach, The Voice newbie Riley Green should not be deterred, as Season 30 is proving to be anyone’s game. Take it from this rock music fan, who’s quickly being won over by one of Team Riley’s country singers. Sure, Kelly has 14-year-old and 16-year-old powerhouse singers on her team – Brianna Cameron, who sang “Reflection” by Christina Aguilera, and Koumba Diallo, who sang the Alicia Key’s hit “Fallin’” – but it’s the teenager on Team Riley that is making the best case for crooning his way to the finals.

Country singer Joe Henley (not to be confused with Joe Hendry) is only 19 and had never played a gig before auditioning for The Voice, which only makes his journey on the show more impressive. After grabbing the attention of Kelly Clarkson and Riley Green during the Blind Auditions, making it through the Battle Rounds, and hands-down reclaiming his spot on Team Riley for Cut Week, he took on Lee Ann Womack’s “I Hope You Dance.”

It's one of those country tracks that has crossed over into the mainstream, with deeply emotional lyrics that I’ve personally connected with and that always pull on my heartstrings when I hear it. It was an unexpected choice to hear the #1 hit covered by a male, but Joe crushed it, reinforcing the possibility that he really could win it all in Season 30.

For a rock girlie to be saying that is a big deal! Just saying!

Sure, Team Adam and Team Kelly have the numbers advantage, with three singers still left on each of their teams while the other coaches only have two. I can’t believe I’m still on the country train, but I actually think that Team has a very good chance of winning in his first season, whether that’s with Joe Henley or the duo Ferryn & Brinkley. He’s proven to have an excellent ear for talent and has given great advice and guidance to his team as their performances have only gotten stronger.

While we already know the competition series will be shaking things up with Season 31’s The Voice: Celebrity, we won’t learn who will take it all in Season 30, and if that could be country singer Joe Henley, until December. So, be sure to keep tuning in to NBC on Mondays at 8 p.m. ET until then.

#3674. PlayStation defeats £2 billion UK lawsuit that alleged Sony forced consumers into "excessive and unfair prices"

12.2 million gamers can be wrong, apparently.

Sony has defeated a major £2 billion UK class action lawsuit concerning the price of games on the PlayStation Store (thanks, TheGameBusiness). The judgment came after a 30-day Competition Appeal Tribunal that took place in London, where PlayStation users claimed Sony had removed "all actual and potential competition" in relation to selling digital games on the console.

The case, brought by Alex Neill, who said she represented roughly 12.2 million gamers, accused Sony of applying "excessive and unfair" pricing on games that appeared on the storefront accessible by PS3, PS4 and PS5 consoles - the PlayStation Store. In a judgment published by the London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal today (17th November), the case was rejected. The judgement noted that market definitions used to define Sony's conduct were "unsafe", and that consumers "would be likely to make informed choices when purchasing consoles" and games on the hardware, too.

"Potential PlayStation console purchasers had both access to sufficient information and an incentive to consider that information in order to make informed purchasing decisions at the console level, especially in the case of high-value users who spend significant amounts in the digital gaming aftermarket," read the judgment.

The lawsuit made the argument that, upon purchasing a PS5 or other PlayStation console, you were then trapped within its ecosystem, and forced into paying the prices determined by Sony. The Tribunal disagreed, however, and ruled that Sony competed within a wider 'systems market' alongside Xbox, Nintendo and PC, for example. Furthermore, the Tribunal found no evidence that the existence of other digital storefronts would have actually brought any PlayStation Store pricing down.

Interestingly, the Tribunal used the argument that consumers can also opt and buy physical games instead of using the PlayStation Store - something that is changing as of the start of 2028. That did not seem to have any bearing on today's decision, though. It's also worth noting that this case did not seek to interrogate the ownership status of digital games - something that's been at the heart of the movement rallying against Sony's decision to kill off physical media. Earlier this year, spokespeople from Sony's legal team argued "reasonable consumers" already know they don't actually own their digital games.

The London Tribunal has a fairly long history. Back in 2022, it began as a case that attempted to sue Sony to the tune of £5bn for "ripping people off" on PlayStation Store. Sony argued the case brought against it in this trial was "flawed from start to finish". This isn't the only situation where we're seeing consumers pursue legal action against the platform holder. Last year, PlayStation was sued in the Netherlands over the so-called "Sony tax" that highlighted artificially inflated prices on the Store, and sought to represent more than 20,000 participants that felt short-changed by the company.

Rockstar's budget doesn't "represent a business model anyone else can or probably should emulate"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rockstar seems to have really, really stuck the landing with GTA 6. After a decade of astronomically high expectations, GTA 6 is launching this week to universal acclaim, tying the original Zelda: Ocarina of Time for highest rated game of all time on Metacritic. As the GTA 6 release time opens up for different players around the world, people are just beginning their rampages around Leonida and sharing new discoveries by the minute. And yet, one very prominent RPG developer hopes we never see the likes of a game the size and scale of GTA 6 ever again.

In a new Linkedin post, Warren Spector, best-known for creating the Deus Ex series, sounds plenty happy for Rockstar fans and developers celebrating a monumental critical achievement, but also concerned about the precedent it might be setting for other game developers.

"First, congratulations to everyone who worked on GTA 6. It looks like it will be a high point of sorts for our medium and our business," Spector says, before pivoting. "However… It’s billion-dollar development cost and an undoubtedly crazy marketing budget don’t represent a business model anyone else can or probably should emulate. That’s especially true when thousands of developers are out of work.

"A billion dollars pays for a lot of games and a lot of salaries. Personally I'd rather have hundreds of games and full employment than one game no matter how amazing it is."

I definitely understand having an instinctual negative reaction to someone saying, quite explicitly, no more GTA ever again, or at least not at the scale of GTA 6, but my read here is that Spector is saying the amount of money that went into the game could support several game studios and hundreds of game developers at a time when game studios and game developers seem to constantly be on the chopping block.

Spector also says GTA 6's success proves a point he's been making "for years," which is that "no game that matters ships on time and/or on budget," pointing again to GTA 6's staggering $1 billion budget and multiple delays.

"Give a game the time and money to prove its potential (key word, potential) and you have a chance of making something great," he says. "Underfund a game or force it out the door before it’s ready guaranteed failure no matter how much potential it has.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

"So, again, congratulations. Ambition and innovation are necessary for the medium to reach its potential. I just hope GTA 6 is the last of its kind even if it’s the best we have to offer."

It's impossible to predict the full economic impact of a game like GTA 6. Even with its incredible reviews, some Rockstar developers are already worrying about potential layoffs now that the game is shipping. On the other hand, GTA 6's inevitable gargantuan commercial success could generate unprecedented revenue and have a reinvigorating effect on the gaming industry as a whole. One thing's for sure, we probably won't see another $1 billion game for a very, very long time, so I guess Spector is getting his wish.

#3672. The Game Awards just confirmed who plays GTA 6's Lucia

Manni L. Perez has been confirmed as the actress behind Grand Theft Auto 6's Lucia Caminos, just days before the game launches.

As spotted by IGN, the confirmation came during The Game Awards' nominations livestream today, where Perez was nominated for Best Performance for her role as co-lead Lucia.

Perez had been widely rumoured to play Lucia for months, and fans have regularly filled her social media livestreams with questions about GTA 6, which she has been oh-so-carefully sidestepping.

Lucia is one half of GTA 6's lead pair alongside Jason Duval, making it the first Grand Theft Auto game with a playable couple.

Jason's actor wasn't among the nominees, so who plays him is still a mystery.

Perez has previously had guest roles in a string of US TV dramas, including Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, Chicago P.D., The Blacklist, and Blindspot, and has also done voice work for GTA Online.

Funnily enough, Lucia isn't her first Lucia - she also played Lucia Santiago in a 2023 episode of CBS's East New York.

GTA 6 arrives 19th November on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. It is now available to pre-load for anyone who pre-ordered the digital version, and those with the code-in-box physical version.

It's long been revealed that GTA 6 will have a regional release, meaning that some lucky, soon-to-be players will be able to access the game much earlier than others. Rockstar's regional release schedule sees the game launching at midnight on 19th November regardless of what region you're in, and if you wish to join those playing almost a day early, there's the good ol' Xbox New Zealand trick for eager players to try.

Cars have gotten smarter, but so have you.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Used to be that all you needed to steal a car in a GTA game was a few seconds and a sharp elbow. In GTA 6, you can still smash a window and hotwire some cars, but the car stealing system has changed a lot and the further you get into the game, the more tools you'll need.

That means a quick getaway in a stolen vehicle isn't always that simple. Here are the methods for stealing cars, the new tools you'll get and when they become available in the story, and everything else you need to know about boosting rides in GTA 6.

Want to steal a car? Walk up to the door and press the interact button. That'll tell you if it's locked (most are), if it's alarmed (nearly all are), and if it's keyless—a new type of car that we'll cover more below.

If you smash the window, you'll then climb into the car and need to hotwire it, which just takes a second or two and uses the control sticks to find the "sweet spot." If it's a keyless car, you won't be able to hotwire it or drive it away—again, more on that below. If you smash a window on an alarmed car, the alarm will sound, which can attract attention.

You can still pull people out of their cars, but be warned: many of them will fight back, meaning you'll need to hammer a button quickly to defeat them. Lose, and they'll clonk your head against the side of the car, knocking you down and speeding away. And even if you do pull them out of their car, this is Leonida: a lot of motorists are armed and aren't shy about opening fire.

You can't slim jim a car someone is already sitting in, so you'll have to break the window if the door is locked. Plus, there are car trackers to worry about now: more on that below.

In Chapter 1, in the sixth story mission called Unwanted Attention, your buddy Cal will help you install the "Waink It" app on your phone, which lets you scan cars to see their make and model, if they're locked, alarmed, keyless, or have trackers. The app will also tell you the condition of the car, how much it can be sold for, and what it costs to register them—registering stolen cars at Pay 'n' Spray shops is how you take ownership of them in GTA 6.

Want to get into a locked car without breaking the window or setting off the alarm? You'll need a slim jim, a tool that lets you pop the lock and open the door quietly.

You'll get this new tool in Chapter 2 of the main story, in the fifth mission called "Moses," where you meet an auto mechanic (Moses!) who will give you a slim jim and teach you how to use it. Now when you sidle up to a car door, you'll be able to use the slim jim to pop the lock: no broken windows, no alarms—though it takes a little longer than using your elbow. Again, you still won't be able to start keyless cars, even if you have a slim jim.

Here's the big one. Keyless cars can't be hotwired, so you'll need a key cloner. You'll get the key cloner in Chapter 3, in the 16th mission called "Steal the Zorruso for Randy." That's a long time to wait, but now you can stand next to the door of a keyless car and use your phone to clone its key.

Bonus: the key cloner will not only unlock the door but automatically start the car. That makes it worth the wait! However, keyless cars often come with another new system: trackers.

Not a big deal, really: if a car has a standard tracker, it just means you can't modify it at a mod shop unless you've paid to register the car as your own. I probably wouldn't modify a car unless I owned it anyway, so I never worried about standard trackers at all.

These can be a problem. Advanced trackers will notify the police that the car has been stolen and pinpoint your location—and the cops will respond quickly. To defeat the advanced tracker, you need to drive fast enough that the tracker won't be able to send a signal to the cops. Slow down, and it'll start beeping and you'll only have a few seconds to speed up again. If you fail to speed up enough, the tracker will pinpoint your location and the cops will be on you again.

You have to drive pretty fast to keep the advanced tracker from triggering, which makes it tougher to get them to a Pay 'n' Spray or a Randy's garage without doing some serious damage to the car. Good luck!

You can sell stolen cars at a Pay 'n' Spray, though there's a limit of three cars per day. You can also sell to your two automobile fences, Moses and Randy, though Moses only buys older model, low-end cars and Randy only buys certain flashy, expensive cars. Your Waink It app will tell you if a car is suitable for sale to either of them.

You can also store stolen cars at a garage if you've purchased one through the real estate app on your phone. Each garage only has room for a single car. You can also use a parking spot or spots outside your current safehouse to store a stolen car.

#3670. Firaxis reportedly cuts a third of its staff as studio head departs and new XCOM struggles

Civilization and XCOM developer Firaxis Games has laid off around 60 people.

The cuts, which took place today, account for about a third of the studio’s staff, Bloomberg reports, citing people familiar with the matter. Studio head Heather Hazen is also leaving.

Its sources say Firaxis' unannounced XCOM game has faced development struggles and missed "a significant milestone over the summer". The project will continue, but "may face a shakeup as a result of the cuts".

A spokesperson for 2K, the Take-Two label that runs Firaxis, confirmed Hazen's departure to Bloomberg, and said the studio is "restructuring and recentering around the studio's core strength - designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years".

"As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis," the spokesperson continued. "These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis."

The layoffs come two days before the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6, which is developed and published by Rockstar, a separate label at Take-Two.

In September, around 18 months after Civ 7's widely criticised launch - and as the legendary 4X series celebrates its 35th anniversary - Firaxis unveiled a host of new updates coming to the game as it continued to improve it. These included an atomic age update, dragging Civ 7 into the present and beyond, as well as its first paid expansion, Earthrise, both arriving next year.

Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick admitted earlier this year that the studio "got it wrong with Civ 7".

"The game is a really good game. And it's certainly a profitable enterprise for us. But this is one where I think what we tried to do was a bridge too far, from the consumer's perspective," he told Game File in May.

It’s not the first round of cuts at the studio - 2K confirmed an unspecified number of layoffs at Firaxis in September 2025, and around 30 jobs went in 2023.

#3669. GTA 6 Finally Explains Why You Can Hear The Police Radio Chatter

If you’ve played any of the mainline Grand Theft Auto games, you’ve likely committed a crime and heard a police radio communication reporting your naughty behavior. It’s been a part of the series since the first game. And yet, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the first game in the series to actually explain how your character can hear this police chatter.

Early on in Grand Theft Auto 6, Jason’s hacker friend and stoner buddy Cal does the character a solid. He grabs his phone and installs a custom, homebrew police radio scanner program. From then on, Jason can hear the police reporting on his actions, crimes, and location, as was the case in (nearly) every previous GTA game. Later on, when GTA 6 lets you free-roam around as Lucia, she, too, has the same police scanner app installed on her phone. The game doesn’t show Cal installing it, so I’ll just assume it happened off-camera.

Now, to be clear, I don’t think Rockstar needed to dedicate any time or effort to explaining how players could hear police radio chatter in GTA. Sure, sometimes I’d think about how it was possible for characters like CJ or Tommy Vercetti to hear the police reporting on their crimes, but then I would just remind myself it’s a video game, and games are filled with stuff that doesn’t make sense. Characters die and then respawn. Protagonists never age. And you can hear the police radio chatter despite not having a scanner. Just usual video game-y nonsense.

Still, I think it’s fun that for GTA 6, Rockstar took the time to explain how Jason and Lucia can hear the police radio chatter. And it also factors into gameplay. Our protagonists know if the police have spotted their car or have reported their clothing. They even mention it during chases as they try to make their escape, so it’s important we understand that the characters, and not just the player, can hear the chatter. In past games, you could just assume it was a gameplay mechanic, and the protagonists didn’t hear the radio messages. Not so in GTA 6.

I guess Rockstar felt like it was finally necessary to provide a grounded explanation for this classic GTA feature.Â I await Rockstar explaining why every state in the GTA universe is an island in Grand Theft Auto 7.Â

What does the future hold for DC Studios?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

To say that DC Studios is in the midst of a big change would be a major understatement. It was announced a little over a week ago that in the aftermath of the Warner Bros./Paramount merger, James Gunn and Peter Safran would step down as co-CEOs of the studio. As a result, film producer (and Marvel Studios alum) Jeremy Latcham will lead the brand moving forward. There may, however, now be reason to believe that DC may be leaving WB and by extension, parent company Skydance. This is all due to some recent rumors.

A common claim that’s been reported in the aftermath of the Gunn/Safran news is that Skydance has acquired a lot of Warner Bros.-amassed debt following the merger. It’s been said that a number of DC Studios’ projects were particularly pricey for the company. In a wide-ranging piece, Page Six mentioned sources who alleged that Supergirl, which flopped at the box office earlier this year, lost WB $135 million. With that, X user @entylawyer alleges that Skydance wants to unload the superhero brand for monetary purposes:

The comic studio heads were fired. They didn't quit. Their boss wants to sell off the entire comic book universe to help get rid of some of that $100B debt.

Of course, all of this should be taken with a massive grain of salt, as Skydance’s David Ellison has not indicated that the company plans to sell DC Studios. If that were to actually happen, though, it would result in the availability of a major asset. If Ellison and co. were to sell it, it could theoretically draw some significant interest on the open market.

I’m honestly just not sure who would seek to acquire DC Studios if Skydance were to theoretically choose to sell it. There’s also the matter of which entertainment company would actually have the money to do it. One of the first brands that comes to mind is obviously The Walt Disney Company, which acquired Marvel Entertainment back in 2009 for $4 billion. However, another brand that should be considered as a hypothetical buyer is Netflix,the company that was set to acquire WB before Paramount made a higher bid.

All of that is just speculation but, of course, James Gunn’s DC exit is real, with him and Peter Safran officially stepping down on December 1. News of Gunn’s departure has generated disappointment from those who were all in on his DC plans, and some have expressed concerns about the future of his DCU continuity. As for the actual decision to part ways with Safran and Gunn, a source for Page Six alleged that their bosses had been in talks with Latcham for weeks ahead of the announcement despite publicly saying otherwise:

It was a little bit strange to have it be so publicly stated that [Gunn and Safran] were safe, and during that time, the [Latcham] process had already been kicked off. They were saying one thing, and then they were actively doing another thing.

Naturally, there are a lot of unknown variables here, and it’s currently unclear as to it or when Skydance might confirm or deny the rumor that DC Studios will be sold. In the meantime, there are still film projects from the brand that are in different stages of development as James Gunn’s Man of Tomorrow is set to hit theaters on July 9 amid the 2027 movie schedule. Matt Reeves’ The Batman: Part II is also filming right now and will hit theaters on February 18, 2028.

#3666. Yes, You Can Keep Playing GTA 6 After The Credits Roll And Don’t Worry, That’s Not A Spoiler

Grand Theft Auto 6 is a very, very big game with tons of main missions, side missions, activities, random events, races, and more to find and complete. So you might feel compelled to clear out the map before reaching the finale. But you don’t need to do that.

In past Rockstar Games, like GTA V and Red Dead Redemption 2, the studio has let players return to the open world after finishing the main story. However, how this has been handled has varied. In RDR2, you take on the role of another character who can complete activities and side missions after the credits roll. In GTA IV, the game just lets you keep playing post-credits as Niko. This is how it works in most GTA games, actually. Things are a bit different in GTA 6.

Instead, before you enter the final mission, which took me about 90 hours or so to reach in my playthrough, the game makes a big point of asking if you want to go forward with the finale or not. Once you wrap up that big, multi-mission finale and see one of the game’s main endings, GTA 6 tosses you back in time to that moment when you were asked if you wanted to finish the story or not. But this time, Jason and Lucia say no; they aren’t ready, and head back out into Vice City. At that point, you can keep playing GTA 6, wrap up everything on the map, and explore. (The finale mission marker remains on the map if you want to finish the game again and possibly get a different ending.)

It’s an interesting way to handle the endgame and is unlike any past Grand Theft Auto. It also lets GTA 6‘s ending go in a lot of different directions, depending on your choices. I’m not going to even hint at what those endings are, but I’ve seen two of them and trust me, they play out in wildly different and sometimes surprising ways.

The one downside to this approach is that GTA 6 feels a bit frozen in time at the end of the game. No new major storylines can be introduced, as they would possibly get in the way of the narrative wrapping up.

But hey, once you beat the final mission, you unlock the ability to reach 100 percent completion and even unlock the ability to complete challenges to reveal in-game cheat codes that let you go wild in Vice City. So consider it a vacation for Jason and Lucia after all your hard work as a criminal.

It's pretty much impossible to describe GTA 6 as anything other than a massive success. It is expected to break commercial records set by GTA 5 and it's tied with only The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as the highest rated game of all time on Metacritic. And yet, because we're living in 2026 after all, many Rockstar developers who helped bring the game to life are now worrying about losing their jobs.

Writing for The Guardian, Rockstar animation programmer Nestor Uriart argues in support of this month's UK-wide Rockstar Games union-recognition ballot, believing unionization is key to "safeguard our jobs."

Games like Battlefield 6, and the layoffs that happened after its commercially successful launch, prove time and time again that strong sales and reviews are nothing compared to shareholder value when it comes to deciding whether or not to implement mass layoffs at a studio backed by a publicly traded company. And yet, you'd think having your name attached to the literal biggest game of all time would get you some sense of job security, but apparently that's not the case for everyone at Rockstar.

"While the highs of a game release like this can be incredible, game workers have also come to expect other, less welcome side effects: intense overtime in the buildup and mass redundancies in the aftermath," writes Uriart, arguing that unionizing could also help address allegations Rockstar has faced in the past of crunch culture. "With a strong union we could make sure there is no return to this system. We have already seen the introduction of some overtime pay, and now we want to keep on pushing to ensure that every hour worked in our industry is an hour paid."

Uriart says there's been "no indication that layoffs are coming, but it’s hard not to worry about what the future holds. Studios across the industry have been slashing huge portions of their workforces, with an estimated 24,000 roles axed globally over the last two years.

"It says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised."

As GTA 6 is just releasing this week, it's impossible to get a picture of the scale of its commercial success. We already know it's the most pre-ordered game of all time, but that was almost a given. Perhaps I'm being naive, but I would like to think it's going to be so overwhelmingly successful that Take-Two holds off on making any large-scale staffing changes. That said, now that development is transitioning into post-launch support, it's reasonable as a developer on the team to worry about downsizing.

#3663. Wow, GTA 6 Has Some Incredible Animations

Grand Theft Auto 6GTA 6Rockstar GamesTiny Details

Grand Theft Auto 6, out now on Xbox and PS5, is a very big game. But don’t assume it’s just a blandly massive world with no tiny details to discover. Rockstar Games has packed GTA 6 with more detail than any of its previous games, including some truly impressive animations.

Let’s start with one of the earliest animations I spotted that truly made me go “Whhhooooaaa…” I parked too close to a car, and Jason was unable to fully open his door. In past GTA games, this would lead to the character teleporting out of the car or the door clipping through the other vehicle. In GTA 6, that’s not the case. Instead, Rockstar has added a dedicated animation for Jason and Lucia where they squeeze in and out of the car.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is filled with tiny animations like this that often made me shake my head and think, “I guess I get why this took so long to make.” For example, there are so many animations connected to eating and drinking in this game. I mean, you can crack open a cold one with one hand while holding and shooting an assault rifle in the other.

I also discovered that Jason and Lucia can eat a burger while holding a soda at the same time and even switch between them whenever. And when your drink is empty, you can toss it in a nearby trash can with a procedural animation that doesn’t always work. I’ve missed the trash before, and I felt like an asshole. Jason and Lucia might be murderers who rob and steal, but they aren’t litterbugs!

One animation that really caught me off-guard happened when I was testing how much damage cars in GTA 6 can take before they stop working. I found an empty parking lot, lined up my car with a nearby wall, and floored the accelerator. I expected to slam into the wall and total the front of my vehicle. Instead…

Again, GTA 6 has so many surprising animations and details. I can’t list them all here because I know I’ve not found them all yet. Maybe I never will? Regardless, I highly recommend you poke around GTA 6 and try stuff out because you’re likely to find some wild detail or tiny animation you’ve never seen before.

And for those who want to see a few more, here’s a video compilation I put together of some tiny animations I spotted while playing GTA 6 over the last few weeks. No spoilers are included in the video below.

Here's how the icon felt after his fight with the celebrity host.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Amidst all the tributes and wonderful stories about Patrick Stewart that hit the internet after his passing, one other viral video stood out. Stewart's fight with actor and comedian James Corden onstage at the 2011 Glamour Awards was a rare public outburst by the legendary Star Trek actor, and one that he deeply regretted as the years passed.

For those unfamiliar, the video went viral back then when Stewart took the stage and criticized Corden, the host, for looking disinterested between awards. Corden told Stewart to "get on with presenting," which then escalated to Stewart telling the audience he could see Corden's belly sticking out from the back row. Corden jabbed back that he could see Stewart "dying" onstage due to his age, and after one odd joke involving the Jonas Brothers, the moment ended. People have seen that, but fewer might know how Stewart felt afterward.

Stewart later expressed deep regret about the incident while speaking about it to Classic FM (via Glamour). The Star Trek actor admitted he'd been drinking, and it all went off the rails once he took the stage:

My part of the evening came late and it was alcohol (that prompted the remark), I'm afraid. I went too far, I was somewhat out of control. I have nothing but admiration for Mr Corden. I still blush in remembrance of it.

Buzzfeed also reported that Stewart said elsewhere he was upset by a comment Corden made toward another actress earlier in the evening. He began to drink and, unfortunately, made comments that he regretted. Fortunately, he also confirmed that he'd spoken to the Corden since then, and they agreed to bury the hatchet.

The resurfaced viral video was the most I've seen of James Corden since he retired from late-night, and based on how he spoke about the event, I'm sure he wasn't thrilled to see it back in the news either. The comedian later said he had zero problem with Sir Patrick Stewart, and said that despite how it looked at the moment, he was not mad:

I couldn't have less of a problem with him. He just went for it, he was unscripted, and I've no idea where it was going... And I wish I hadn't looked like I was so angry. Because I was just bemused. I'm not entirely sure what he wanted to happen, but I'm sure what happened wasn't what he wanted. But you know, he's Sir Patrick Stewart and he's great. Everyone's allowed a mistake. My hunch is he's a nice guy.

It's important to know the context of how both sides felt after the fact, because unfortunately, I think people unfairly pushed a narrative about the interaction that wasn't true. The implication was that Patrick Stewart hated James Corden, who has been a polarizing figure since stepping into the limelight.

In reality, the moment went down as one of Stewart's biggest embarrassments, and went against many of the other pleasant interactions that the world knew him for. I'm glad that he found the time to reconcile with Corden after what happened all those years ago, but it's sad to see it resurface again after his death.

CinemaBlend continues to pay respects to Patrick Stewart and offers condolences to his friends and family as they mourn his death. I'm sure more stories about the actor will surface ahead of his appearance in Avengers: Doomsday, which is out in theaters on December 18th.

#3661. Former GTA 4 and Red Dead boss thinks "we are one Toy Story moment away" from people accepting gen-AI in game development in the West

"In the East, they've already accepted it."

Ben Feder, the former Take-Two CEO who oversaw the launch of massive hits like Grand Theft Auto 4, Red Dead Redemption, Borderlands, and BioShock during his tenure, believes the resistance against gen-AI in games will vanish once the games industry has its 'Toy Story moment'.

"When animation went from hand-drawn to computer animation, there was a massive wall of resistance," Feder told The Game Business. "People didn't think it looked good. Then Pixar launched Toy Story. They created a movie that not only was awesome, but used computer-generated animation and chose a subject matter that made the most of it, and did an amazing job with it."

Feder argued that the success of Toy Story ended the resistance against computer-generated animation, and the same could happen to games. Feder added, "My own view is that we are one Toy Story moment away from consumer acceptance of AI in video games in the West. In the East, they've already accepted it."

Feder, who currently heads up venture capital fund Tirta Ventures, is investing in AI-first games. He, however, doesn't necessarily believe AI will reduce development costs, but that it also offers other advantages that could help game makers keep up with shifting consumer tastes.

"A lot of incumbents think about AI as a way of reducing costs, which it is," Feder said. "I query whether it will actually reduce costs, or will it just make games bigger for the same cost? But we're more interested in what AI can do to radically change gameplay."

Feder views gen-AI simply as new technology that allows developers to do things they couldn't before. He likened it to Unreal Engine's instancing technology, which allowed Fortnite and other battle royale games to support 100+ players in a single server.

"That's question number one as we think about what we invest in: Was this possible before AI?" Feder said of his VC firm's strategy. "And when AI gets better, does the game get better? That's harder for an incumbent to focus on, because they deploy a lot of capital, have enormous advantages in terms of distribution, capital, and IP, and all of that needs to be protected."

There's been enormous pushback from players, developers and pundits against the use of gen-AI in games. Even so, more and more studios have revealed using some gen-AI during development, such as to assist with coding. More broadly, gen-AI adoption is on the rise across the industry, with a recent report estimating 40 percent of developers are using it.

Some development studios, such as Fortnite maker Epic Games, have doubled down on the use of gen-AI in game development. Epic is even more bullish on gen-AI in its Unreal Engine, which the company is currently transforming into an engine that's almost entirely driven by gen-AI and LLMs. Consumer sentiment remains sour, however, and the perception of the tool is not helped by the number of 'AI slop' games taking over Steam's storefront, the 'enshittification' of fan wikis, or the link AI seems to have to the unprecedented wave of layoffs that has shaken the industry over the past two years.

#3660. How Long Is GTA 6? Depends On How You Play

As I prepare to pick up and play Grand Theft Auto VI tonight, I’m bracing myself to be in Leonida pretty much non-stop for days, weeks, maybe even months. It just intuitivelyÂ feels like it’s going to be a doozy of a long game, huh?

After all its predecessor, GTA V, takes 32 hoursÂ just to rush through the main story (according to HowLongToBeat), and over 50 if you factor in side content. I’d expect its successor, especially with all the bells and whistles Rockstar is showing off, to take even longer.

With reviews out today, we now have a rough idea of what to expect, and yeah: this game’s gonna take time.

Our own reviewer, Zack, says he saw the credits roll at about 90 hours of gameplay. Granted, he was doing a lot of side content and wandering around and testing stuff, and not everyone will want to be anywhere near as thorough as he was. Zack suggests a speedier player might make it through in around 60 hours. Jeff Gerstmann, in his review, says he beat the game after about 45 hours, maybe 50 if you count some saves he had to reload throughout. Zack doesn’t think you can reasonably finish the story in much less than that.

For those looking for more to do, though, Zack has spent 150 hours in GTA VI and still hasn’t seen everything there is to see or done everything there is to do. Like past Rockstar games, GTA VI will let you keep playing after the credits roll (though in a slightly unusual way), so you’re free to turn Leonida inside out for days on end if that’s what you want to do.

Sorry to all the other games in my backlog, we might be here a while.

Even though Grand Theft Auto 6 will be taking over the world tomorrow, World of Warcraft: Forever was the first game this month that people flocked to in record-breaking numbers.

While we don't know the exact player count like we do with games on Steam, we can make an educated guess on just how many people dove into the MMO via a recent set of statistics from Blizzard. According to the official WoW X account, over 15 million characters were created in the last few weeks.

Characters aren't individual players. You can create dozens of characters on your account if you want to, but I'd guess most people didn't do that. This is a game where you can put hundreds of hours into one character before ever reaching the level cap. There definitely aren't 15 million total players based on this statistic, but the number might not be massively below that.

I can't say I'm surprised that a spin-off MMO that will remain stuck in the most universally nostalgic era of WoW was a big hit. Everyone who stopped playing for one reason or another came back to remember what it was like to smack a scorpion for 38 seconds.

Whether or not they'll stick around is the question. Blizzard plans on updating the game with new things to do for players at different stages of the long leveling journey. Most people are still weeks away from reaching the level 60 cap, partially because there are so many things to do that don't involve XP. The first raid is around the corner, but I'm curious to see what kind of stuff is added for those of us who are still chilling in the mid-30s. It'd better be good because many of us will be on vacation in Leonida for the next several weeks.

#3658. Blizzard suspends World of Warcraft: Forever gold exploit abusers, puts trading blocks on their accounts and removes ill-gotten funds for good measure

Players who abused World of Warcraft: Forever's Blackmaw Hold unintended gold farm, which allowed a small minority of players to hoard thousands of gold in a few days, have drawn the ire of WoW publisher, Blizzard. Suspensions have been issued, trade locks have been put on accounts, and ill-gotten gold is being seized.

For those unaware, the World of Warcraft: Forever community was greatly alarmed by this gold farm, which had players clear the same non-elite enemies from the new late game dungeon, Blackmaw Hold. By quickly clearing select mobs with area-of-effect damage, players would loot upwards of 100 raw gold an hour. This exploit, clearly not intentional, was nonetheless farmed until Blizzard hotfixed it earlier in the week.

There was much speculation on what would happen to those who participated in this exploit. That speculation would come to an end late last night with an official statement from the World of Warcraft: Forever development team.

"As players continue their journey into WoW Forever’s higher-level content, we are closely monitoring the game economy to ensure that gold sources and costs are well balanced," the statement reads. "Finding efficient farming spots has always been part of the game, and is how most players have earned their epic mounts since 2004. When a single location proves so lucrative that it overshadows all other sources, we generally adjust it to bring it in line with the rest."

It goes on to explain the nature of the bug that made this gold farm possible, before reassuring those who may have accidentally benefited from some extra cash from their regular runs of Blackmaw Hold they have nothing to worry about. The same cannot be said for those who took advantage of the situation.

"Players who simply ran Blackmaw Hold a few times and benefited organically from the extra loot did nothing wrong, and no one should worry that they’re putting their account at risk if they accidentally benefit from a bug," it continues. "But there were a couple hundred players worldwide who recognized that this was unintended and spent significant time exclusively farming that group of enemies.

"Yesterday, we put an economy lock on their accounts to prevent broader impact to the game economy while we investigated the extent of the exploitative gains, including gold earned by vendoring bugged drops. Today, we are in the process of removing all such gold earned, as well as applying account suspensions to significant abusers."

The post concludes by thanking players for their feedback on the matter, and a final warning: "As always, we advise all players to refrain from abusing game mechanics that are clearly unintended. We will continue to take action against intentional abuse."

This decision certainly sets the precedent moving forward with World of Warcraft: Forever that such exploits won't be tolerated, and rolling back the wealth of those who made out of Blackmaw Hold like bandits is a good measure that should prevent continuous damage.

Inevitably the exploit would have had some impact, specifically in those days prior to trading blocks being put in place. While the gold on the exploiter's accounts may be removed, any purchases they made on the in-game auction house will have affected others through buying and selling goods with ample funds.

Those who were suspended temporarily will be able to regain access to the game by the time the first wave of raids come out in December, so it very much feels like a firm slap on the wrist in that regard. Even so, given the establishment of punishments for such behavior, one can only wonder if future events will come with harsher penalties.

World of Warcraft: Forever, despite this small economic roadbump, is proving exceptionally popular for Blizzard. It's already broken records for the series, and has impressed players so far with its revamping of the classic MMO.

#3657. TGAs Nominating A Game That’s Been Left To Die Shows What A Weak Year It Was for Fighting Games

2XKOAvatar Legends: The Fighting GameThe Game Awards

The nominees for this year’s Game Awards have been announced. GTA VI has (rightfully) racked up a bunch of noms, as have Control Resonant and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. But there’s a lot of head-scratching going on at the games nominated for Best Fighting Game, shining an uncomfortable light on how anemic the genre has gotten outside of the big twoâTekken and Street Fighter.

Nominated for Best Fighting Game 2026 are Marvel TÅkon: Fighting Souls, Invincible Vs, 2XKO, Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game, and My Hero Academia: All’s Justice.

Woof. Let’s break down these nominees. 2XKO is dead, with active development ending on the game at the end of December, a few short weeks after the Game Awards take place. Invincible Vs has had its development team busted down to a “skeleton crew.” The Avatar Legends team features a developer accused of sexual harassment and is a part of the currently shrinking Paramount Games thanks to the Skydance merger. I’m not sure that many people even knew about All’s Justice, which feels like it was thrown in there to pad out the list.

It’s hard to make a fighting game viable. NetherRealm’s Mortal Kombat 1 earned favorable player sentiment when it was released in 2023, but the game fell off so hard in the years since that EVO 2026 marked the first time a NetherRealm game hadn’t been featured in the main event lineup since 2011. It seems like nearly every new fighting game fails either before or right after it launches. (Paging Multiversus.) Even Marvel TÅkon, which will almost assuredly win the category, seems to be facing an uphill sales and concurrent player battle to stay alive.

And yes, that’s true of 95 percent of games in this day and age, but fighting games are one of the genres particularly sensitive to that pressure. It’s almost miraculous that Keighley was even able to drum up enough games to flesh out the category at all. And I don’t know how much longer he’ll be able to do that for.

"One perk of seeing the sun first? Getting GTA 6 first too," reads a post on the New Zealand tourist board's Instagram account: PureNewZealand. Microsoft has for years been happy to let this practice continue on its platform, and as such a sort of cultural norm about hopping on a digital plane for a game's release has been established. There are few things I love more than a reality show, and after years of devouring The Traitors with my Peacock subscription, I was thrilled to hear that the folks behind that Emmy-winning series were creating another. Enter The Mob, another campy competition show that's available in its entirety with a Hulu subscription. The show once again proved that RuPaul's Drag Race alum Willam Belli is a top-tier TV personality, but it turns out that not even the cast knew the rules when cameras went up.

The Mob's jobs feel more urgent than The Traitors' missions, but it took some adjusting to its format. Even the cast had a hard time with this, mostly because they didn't actually know all of the rules of the show they were competing on. During a recent clip from Gayety's Instagram, Willam spoke about her experience shooting the series, saying:

I asked for the rules every episode and I didn't get them until Episode 4, a printed copy. We did not know what was going on and we really wanted to. But information is power, and I understand that you don't want a reality show contestant to have power. So keeping them in dark leads to better stakes for the game and I understand that now.

Well, my mind is blown. It was hard enough to nail down the rules and format of The Mob as a viewer, but the fact that the cast was similarly clueless is truly wild to me. It didn't make the show's first four episodes any less entertaining, even though many of my favorite contestants got whacked way too early. Still, I'd think that the powers that be on production would want the reality TV personalities to at least know everything about the game they were expected to play.

As much as I enjoyed the first season of The Mob, I have to assume that the gameplay might have been even more dynamic if the cast knew the show's rules from the jump. Indeed, the first few eliminations were a little sleepy, such as Dancing with the Stars judge Bruno Tonioli pledging allegiance to Joe Gorga and then immediately getting whacked.

You can see Willam Belli's comments about The Mob and feeling a bit clueless at the start of filming below:

Willam might be the only contestant from RuPaul's Drag Race to get disqualified, but that doesn't mean she went against the rules in every situation. After all, The Mob cast were starting a brand new competition series, and didn't have any previous episodes to use as a reference. The folks who caught on seemed to make it the farthest, but it was curtains for other favorites like Willam, Bruno, and Debi Mazar.

The Mob is streaming in its entirety on Hulu as part of the 2026 TV schedule. We'll just have to see if it gets renewed for a second season, and how the gameplay changes with contestants who know what to expect.

#3654. Slay the Spire 2 is one of this year's best selling games despite only being available on PC, and its players are "obsessed"

One million copies for each month on sale, it seems. Slay the Spire 2, Mega Crit's roguelike deckbuilder, is estimated to have sold 7.9m copies since its release in Steam Early Access in March.

That's according to estimates by Alinea Analytics industry analyst Rhys Elliott, who revealed in a LinkedIn post that those sales translate to $157.6m (~£119.6m) in revenue for the small studio.

Slay the Spire 2 is now the sixth best-selling 2026 release across Steam, PlayStation and Xbox. That is notable, as the game is only out on Steam, meaning it has sold enough copies to outpace games on platforms it's not even available on.

We already knew Slay the Spire 2 was one of the year's biggest releases. In its first week on sale, the game sold over 3m copies. It quickly became March's top-selling game on Steam, beating blockbuster competition in Crimson Desert and Resident Evil Requiem. Slay the Spire 2, alongside other indie titles such as Meccha Chameleon, have helped Steam deliver another record year of revenue.

It was such a hit, even, that other indie developers felt it negatively impacted sales of their own games. Mewgenics maker Edmund McMillen recently told Eurogamer "it sucked everybody out". "The same players who liked Mewgenics, they were Slay The Spire players. So they all went woosh and right over," McMillen said.

Slay the Spire 2 has been consistently popular with players, too, and that popularity has seemingly continued. Elliott noted the game never fell below 2.5 million active players each month since March.

Slay the Spire 2's loyal following also meant that the recently released beta patch, which added a new character, was enough to bring back millions of players. Despite only being available for players who opt into the beta branch of the game, Slay the Spire 2 more than doubled its daily active users to reach its highest daily player count in six months.

"Simply put: Slay the Spire 2 players are obsessed," wrote Elliott. "And it's not just a niche group of dedicated players, either. The average play time is nearly 84 hours, sure. But zooming out, 1.9 million folks have played for over 100 hours."

Incidentally, nearly 100,000 players bought the game but never played it, which Elliott added could explain the discrepancy between player numbers and copies sold.

Looking ahead, Slay the Spire 2's road to version 1.0 is expected to be long, with several features and gameplay additions still in the works. Then there are the console ports, which have yet to be announced, but are very much expected.

In Eurogamer's Slay the Spire 2 early access review, Bertie Purchese called it "a deceptively familiar sequel" whose confident design and smart new additions build on what made the original work so well.

It's here. GTA 6 has been loosed upon the world, and another nation's productivity goes dark as each advancing hour unleashes midnight unlocks on the next timezone. And hey, from the sounds of it, people seem to like what they're finding—and they're finding a lot.

You can mini-golf. You can go on beach dates. You can text and drive (don't). You can doomscroll, and birdwatch, and ride a jetski with a dog. GTA 6 is dense with possible activities, actions, systems, and mechanics, but not everyone is having the best luck navigating the maelstrom of associated controls and button prompts. Allow me to present Japanese X user @Shunep3_STS, who on this day represents all of us:

操作が増えて覚えきれず、間違えて２つ買ったシェイクをしゃがみ歩きしながら飲み干すヤバい奴になってる https://t.co/OLXaEQGc7CNovember 18, 2026

"There are so many new controls I can’t keep them all straight," said @Shunep3_STS via machine translation, "and now I’m that guy chugging two shakes I accidentally bought while walking around in a squat."

There's something magical about this image. To begin with, the scene—like all of GTA 6—looks profoundly, almost grotesquely expensive: the delicate feathering of Jason's forearm hair, the pseudo-memoji of Cal in the text message notification, the fidelity of pebbled sand that probably cost more to realize in-game than I've spent on rent in the last three years. It's a tableau of technological excess.

And all of that's being deployed to present a man double-fisting slushies in an empty parking lot as he skulks like an imperiled raccoon. Look at him! Look at his face! He's got his chiseled jaw set like he's Solid Snake, but he's nursing a tummy full of iced corn syrup because the pilot controlling his body got too overwhelmed by which buttons do what.

And he's not alone: Our own Andrea Shearon is one of the many struggling to keep up with the sheer volume of button prompts in GTA 6. "There's so much going on," she said. "I just walk up to people and kind of mash all the face buttons for a surprise. You never know if I'm gonna punch someone or do squats or flip them off."

She's spent a lot of time accidentally making rude gestures at her snake as a result.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Amidst all the breathless praise, clips of psychopathic violence, reactionary outrage-mongering, and general noise coming out of GTA 6's launch, @Shunep3_STS's moment of shame feels very pure. It's a universal experience: No matter how much a game is hyped up, no matter how much money is spent on making it look as impressive as humanly and technologically possible, no matter how much we might want it to, we all inevitably find a way to fumble the controls so badly that the illusion entirely breaks down.

We're all, at some point, a man huddling in the dark, trying to figure out how to put down his sippy cups.

#3652. Clair Obscur's narrative lead has left developer Sandfall Interactive after "wrapping up some final stuff for Expedition"

Last night, it was revealed that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's lead narrative designer, Jennifer Svedberg-Yen, won a BAFTA Breakthrough US award for her contribution to the hit 2025 game, which made history after winning 12 Game Award nominations last year. In the aftermath of her win, Svedberg-Yen dropped a pretty big bombshell: she's no longer with the game's developer, Sandfall Interactive.

"No, I left Sandfall in July, after wrapping up some final stuff for Expedition," she told Gamesbeat when asked if she's still with the company. "We've parted ways." As to what Svedberg-Yen is doing next, she offered a cryptic answer, including talk of writing "my own projects, my own stories". She also discussed another project she's set her sights on: establishing a fund to help mentor and grow a new generation of video game narrative designers.

"One of the initiatives I want to build is a narrative investment fund to focus on narrative-focused game creators, trying to bridge the gap between the seed stage and going to publishers," she explained, noting her background working in finance and how that dovetails nicely with her more recent experience as a narrative lead. "This is the chicken and egg question a lot of people face. To get money from publishers you need a demo, but to make a demo you need money. To get money you have to go to publishers. That’s an area where I would like to help a lot of these smaller creatives to get that seed funding so they can, in a way, de-risk themselves in the eyes of bigger investors."

Her motivation for this initiative? Simply, she wants to change how the industry works. "I've discovered that quite a lot of studios don’t really know how to think about narrative, or how to integrate it into their pipelines and their processes. They tend to think it's a very narrow thing, when in fact it can influence all aspects. Part of this would also be an incubation program to help these studios develop those narrative foundations."

"The strongest feeling in me right now for 2027 is I want to help," she added later. "That sounds so cheesy and idealistic. I always cringe at myself for saying it. But I don't know how else to say it and be truthful. I want to help in some way, help the industry."

Sandfall Interactive previously said its guiding "North Star" will always be its "own personal taste", and what the team enjoys.She noted that she didn't think the studio would bow to pressure from fans to do more of the same, but instead be guided by what it thinks is best for itself, and for the series. "I've seen too many TV shows and books be swayed trying to please a lot of people, and in the process you end up losing the heart of what's there," she noted.

We know that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is "not the end" of the franchise, and it seems that whatever happens next, it'll have at least a little bit of Svedberg-Yen's creativity instilled in it. I wish her the best for whatever her next step is.

It's a wild time for the superhero genre, specifically on the DC side of things. James Gunn's departure as co-CEO of the studio broke the internet, and fans who spent years watching the DC movies in order have countless questions about what comes next. I've been especially curious about the future of The Penguin (which is streaming with a HBO Max subscription), and now we have an idea about what's going on behind the scenes.

The Penguin is a spinoff of The Batman, and became an Emmy-winning hit after it arrived on HBO. The TV series made me way more invested in Matt Reeves' franchise, and I desperately want a sophomore season to be green lit. During Deadline's recent report about where things stand at DC, it claims that The Penguin showrunner Lauren LeFranc is "in talks" to produce a Poison Ivy series. Unfortunately, the studio is focused on The Batman: Part II before it can plan any potential return to The Penguin.

The Batman: Part II is in the midst of filming, following delays and Matt Reeves' departure due to a family issue. Amidst leadership shakeups, the studio is seemingly focused on getting that title in the can. Fingers crossed that we we get more of The Penguin whenever that movie is finally completed.

The idea of Lauren LeFranc producing a Poison Ivy TV series is a thrilling one, although that developing project isn't set within the Matt Reeves Batman universe. I'll be sat if/when that show comes to life, but I also really need to see more of The Penguin, particularly Cristin Milioti's Sofia Falcone/ The Hangman.

Sofia was one of the main protagonists of The Penguin, and the actress' performance was incredible and earned her an Emmy Award. Unfortunately, Milioti won't be part of The Batman: Part II, despite her popularity among fans. What's more, Colin Farrell claimed he's only in two scenes of the forthcoming sequel. So why not put Cobblepot and Falcone center stage for a second installment of the acclaimed HBO series?

Right now there are countless questions about upcoming DC movies, and what's coming next for the burgeoning DC Universe. We're currently only a few installments into the original plans for Gunn's first slate of projects, titled Gods and Monsters. His replacement Jeremy Latcham is expected to start his run as the new CEO of the studio on December 1st, so maybe we'll get more information then.

As of now, The Batman: Part II is expected to arrive in theaters on February 18th, 2028. If we have to wait that long before getting more news about The Penguin's future, fans like me are going to have to continue practicing patience. Give us more of Sofia Falcone, you cowards!

#3650. Zara Tindall Shows Cheltenham Why She's The Queen of Race Day Dressing

Zara Tindall didn’t let the cold snap stop her from enjoying a day at the races on Friday. Accompanied by her close friend Dolly Maude and country-set favorite fashion designer Jade Holland Cooper, the daughter of Princess Anne and granddaughter of Queen Elizabeth II brought a dash of regal glamour to the proceedings following a glitzy night out in support of Prince William.

And while the sun may have been out, the Olympic equestrian still needed to wrap up against the chill. Tindall opted for a long plaid coat from L'Agence, a Purdey roll-neck jumper in brown, and a fascinator from Sally-Ann Provan. She accessorized with a new pair of Hector Lion earrings, a new Fairfax & Favor handbag, and completed the look with leather boots, also from Fairfax & Favor.

Zara Tindall joined in the action at Cheltenham Racecourse on Friday

Dolly, on the other hand, wore an avant-garde feather coat with knee-high boots and what looked to be a pair of emerald tights.

The pair were last spotted together in October, when they attended the William Hill Showcase Meeting at Cheltenham, but their friendship goes way back. Long considered Zara’s best friend, Dolly became Princess Anne’s lady-in-waiting in 2024. A former NHS midwife, she helped to deliver Zara’s third child, Lucas Tindall, on the floor of Zara’s bathroom at Gatcombe Park after the plan for the birth went awry in 2021.

Jade Holland Cooper and Zara Tindall on day one of The November Meeting at Cheltenham racecourse

But Dolly’s bond with the niece of King Charles III goes back long before that. (Not for nothing did Zara’s husband, Mike Tindall, joke that the 53-year-old is “more important than I am.”) Dolly was Zara’s maid of honor when the pair tied the knot, and when Zara split from her then-fiancé, jockey Richard Johnson, in 2003, the pair moved in together—they still live close by in the Cotswolds.

Having worked as a maternity practitioner in the NHS in Gloucestershire for 13 years, Dolly also did some philanthropic work using her maternity expertise, working in the unit of a hospital in Kambia, Sierra Leone for a month in 2013. At Kambia, she taught staff basic nursing skills. Before qualifying as a nurse, Dolly studied fashion and Cordon Bleu cookery at Eastbourne College of Food and Fashion, graduating in 1989.

Zara Tindall also braved the stormy weather for a day at Cheltenham with Dolly in October

Dolly Maude is known for her love of horses—a passion she shares with Zara and Princess Anne—and is often seen in Ascot’s royal box alongside the Princess Royal. In March 2024, she made her first official appearance as the Princess Royal’s lady-in-waiting, a momentous occasion that marked a new phase of her enduring bond with the royal family.

The royal confidant has four children with her husband Chris: Billy, who studied at Swansea University; Nell, who trained at the Central School of Ballet; a keen skier, Ted; and Mary.

Princess Anne's daughter wrapped up in a warm plaid coat and roll-neck jumper

Concerning Dolly’s appointment, another friend of Mrs. Maude's told The Telegraph, “She’s such a great girl. For the Princess Royal, it’s a perfect fit because of their shared love of dogs and horses. She’s not only extremely close to Zara, she also gets on brilliantly with the Princess. She’s fiercely loyal and discreet. It’s a great match.”

While much of Zara Tindall’s time this season has been spent touring the country’s most prestigious racing meets, she still found time to support her cousin, Prince William, at one of his treasured annual traditions. The Prince of Wales helped to put together the Tusk Conservation Awards at Raffles on Wednesday night and invited Zara to the celebration of conservation, alongside Lady Amelia and Lady Eliza Spencer and the Marchioness of Bath.

Dolly Maud made her debut as lady-in-waiting for the Princess Royal at the 2024 Commonwealth Day Service in March

Zara showcased her characteristically elegant style, donning a sapphire-blue Rebecca Vallance short-sleeved midi number, aptly named the “Crown Jewel” dress, which she paired with Kiki McDonough earrings. It is not the first time that the royal has lent her support to Prince William’s second-longest patronage: she also joined the crowd at the Tusk Awards in 2025, donning Rebecca Vallance again, and tearing up at the Prince of Wales’ speech in honor of those who gave their lives as rangers.
